buckets.title: Sound
buckets.badge_reason: The hard moves are separating source vibration from medium propagation, particle oscillation from disturbance travel, reading graph axes correctly, and treating echo timing as a round trip.

conventions.statement: Name the source, the material medium and the propagation direction before describing a sound wave.
Distinguish a spatial snapshot of the medium from a time trace measured at one location.

scope.covers: Grade-9 sound production/medium reasoning; longitudinal compressions and rarefactions; wave quantities and v=fλ in one medium; pitch/loudness/audible-range distinction; reflection, echo, reverberation and echolocation timing.

capabilities.action: Explain sound production by vibration using strings, membranes and vibrating air columns, and explain why mechanical sound propagation requires a material medium.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identifies the vibrating element in string, membrane and air-column examples, distinguishes source vibration from propagation through solids/liquids/gases, and rejects ordinary sound propagation through vacuum.

capabilities.action: Distinguish local particle oscillation from longitudinal propagation of compressions and rarefactions.
capabilities.success_criterion: Represents alternating compressions and rarefactions, states that medium particles oscillate locally mainly parallel to propagation, and does not draw particles travelling with the disturbance.

capabilities.action: Analyse spatial and temporal sound-wave graphs, relate period, frequency, wavelength, amplitude and speed, and derive v = lambda/T = f lambda for one wave in one medium.
capabilities.success_criterion: Reads graph axes before extracting amplitude, wavelength or period; uses f=1/T and v=fλ only for quantities from the same wave/medium state; distinguishes spatial repeat distance from temporal repeat time.

capabilities.action: Connect frequency with pitch, distinguish sound strength/intensity from pitch, and classify frequencies relative to the approximate human audible range.
capabilities.success_criterion: Uses frequency for pitch, keeps loudness conceptually separate, and treats roughly 20 Hz–20 kHz as an approximate typical human audible range rather than a universal hard boundary.

capabilities.action: Explain reflection of sound and distinguish echo, reverberation and echolocation; compute a simple echo distance from round-trip delay.
capabilities.success_criterion: Traces the outward-and-return path before calculation, uses half the round-trip distance for a stationary reflector, and distinguishes a separate echo from overlapping reverberation without treating one threshold distance as universal.

microtopics.title: Sound starts with vibration and travels through a material medium
microtopics.badge_reason: The key distinction is between the vibrating source and the medium carrying the disturbance.
entry_assumptions: Can identify repeated back-and-forth motion and can distinguish matter from empty space.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A string, stretched membrane or enclosed air column can vibrate and launch a mechanical disturbance into nearby matter; sound then propagates through gases, liquids or solids, but not through a vacuum because there are no material particles to transmit the disturbance.

teaching_path.action: Identify the object that vibrates when sound is produced.
teaching_path.why_valid: Sound production begins with a source undergoing repeated mechanical motion.
teaching_path.output: source: vibrating object.

teaching_path.action: Compare three sound sources—a plucked string, a struck stretched membrane, and a blown air column—and identify what is actually vibrating in each.
teaching_path.why_valid: The current Grade 9 curriculum explicitly varies the sound-producing system; the common invariant is a vibrating physical source.
teaching_path.output: string instrument -> stretched string vibrates; drum-like source -> stretched membrane vibrates; blown pipe/bottle-like source -> enclosed air column vibrates.

teaching_path.action: Follow how neighboring particles in a gas, liquid or solid can push/pull on nearby particles without travelling all the way to the listener.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mechanical interactions between neighboring particles can transmit a disturbance through matter.
teaching_path.output: medium particles move locally; disturbance propagates through the material.

teaching_path.action: Remove the material medium in a thought experiment and ask what interaction remains to carry ordinary sound.
teaching_path.why_valid: A vacuum contains no material particles for the mechanical disturbance to pass between.
teaching_path.output: vacuum -> no ordinary mechanical sound propagation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The vibrating source's particles travel all the way to the listener carrying the sound.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: When a loudspeaker makes sound across a room, do air molecules from the speaker travel across the room to your ear?
misconceptions.repair: Track one small region of air: particles oscillate locally while the disturbance passes from neighbor to neighbor.

exit_task.prompt: A plucked string, a struck drum membrane, and a blown air column all produce sound. Identify the vibrating source in each, then explain what happens to ordinary sound transmission if the surrounding material medium is removed.

answer.summary: The stretched string, stretched membrane and air column are the respective vibrating sources. Their vibration can launch sound into a material medium, but ordinary mechanical sound propagation tends to none as that surrounding medium is removed.
reasoning: In the string example, the stretched string vibrates.
In the membrane example, the stretched membrane vibrates.
In the wind/air-column example, the air column vibrates.
These source vibrations disturb neighboring material particles.
Removing the transmitting material removes the ordinary mechanical path even though a source may still vibrate.
answer.check: The same source-medium distinction works across all three production methods; the vibrating element changes, but the need for a material transmission path does not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit identifies curriculum-named vibrating sources and the qualitative need for a material propagation medium.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 sound-source and medium construction.

predict.prompt: If a bell keeps vibrating while the surrounding air is removed, must the heard sound stay unchanged?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The source can keep vibrating while the medium needed for ordinary sound propagation disappears.

attempt.produces: A source/medium distinction and one vacuum prediction.

rubric.criterion: Keeps source vibration separate from propagation.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing that the source can move even if sound cannot travel through vacuum.

rubric.criterion: Names a material medium as necessary for ordinary mechanical sound.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the propagation mechanism rather than saying sound is an object moving through space.

accepted: Plucked string -> string vibrates; struck drum -> membrane vibrates; blown pipe/bottle -> air column vibrates; sound still requires a material medium to propagate.
rejected: No air means the bell cannot vibrate at all.

boundary_test.answer: No.
boundary_test.confirms: Mechanical sound needs a material medium even though the source itself can vibrate.

microtopics.title: Sound propagates through a medium as longitudinal compressions and rarefactions
microtopics.badge_reason: A transverse-looking sketch is tempting; the learner must keep local particle displacement parallel to propagation and read compression/rarefaction as density/pressure-pattern changes rather than travelling particles.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish a local particle from a propagating disturbance in a medium.
microtopics.inferential_jump: In a simple sound wave through a fluid, neighboring particles oscillate locally mainly parallel to propagation, creating alternating high-density/high-pressure compressions and low-density/low-pressure rarefactions while the disturbance advances.

teaching_path.action: Draw one propagation axis through the medium, mark particle equilibrium positions, and label the propagation direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Longitudinal motion is defined relative to the propagation axis and local equilibrium positions.
teaching_path.output: propagation axis plus local equilibrium positions

teaching_path.action: Displace neighboring particles back and forth mainly parallel to that axis and mark where particles bunch together and spread apart.
teaching_path.why_valid: Local longitudinal oscillation creates alternating regions of higher and lower particle density/pressure.
teaching_path.output: compression = denser/higher-pressure region; rarefaction = less-dense/lower-pressure region

teaching_path.action: Advance the compression-rarefaction pattern while keeping one marked particle near its equilibrium region.
teaching_path.why_valid: The wave/disturbance propagates through successive interactions; matter oscillates locally rather than travelling source-to-listener with the pattern.
teaching_path.output: pattern travels; marked particle oscillates locally

teaching_path.action: Compare the particle-oscillation arrow with the propagation arrow and reject any sketch that makes the fluid particles oscillate primarily perpendicular to propagation.
teaching_path.why_valid: For the simple longitudinal sound model in a fluid, particle displacement is parallel to the propagation direction.
teaching_path.output: particle motion parallel to propagation in the model

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Air particles travel from the source to the listener at the speed of sound.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Follow one marked air particle while a compression travels across the room. Does that same particle travel to the listener?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the particle near its equilibrium region, oscillating locally while the compression/rarefaction pattern passes onward.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Because wave diagrams often look sinusoidal, air particles in sound must move up and down perpendicular to the wave direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: In a simple sound wave travelling right through air, which direction is the local particle displacement mainly along?
misconceptions.repair: Use the propagation axis itself: particles oscillate back and forth mainly parallel to it, producing compressions and rarefactions.

exit_task.prompt: A sound wave travels right through air. Sketch or describe one compression and one rarefaction, then describe the motion of one marked air particle as the pattern passes. State whether the particle motion is parallel or perpendicular to propagation.

answer.summary: The compression is a locally denser/higher-pressure region and the rarefaction a less-dense/lower-pressure region. A marked air particle oscillates locally back and forth mainly parallel to the rightward propagation direction rather than travelling with the wave.
reasoning: Neighboring particle displacements create alternating crowded and spread-out regions.
Those regions form the travelling disturbance pattern.
Each particle remains near its equilibrium region while oscillating.
The local oscillation is mainly parallel to propagation in the longitudinal model.
answer.check: If the marked particle is redrawn kilometres downstream with the same compression, the sketch has confused matter motion with wave propagation.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit describes qualitative particle and disturbance directions only.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted into Grade9V3 from prior internal acoustics engineering, retaining compression/rarefaction representation invariants and rejecting donor release authority.

predict.prompt: When a sound pulse reaches you across a room, must the same air particles that touched the speaker have reached your ear?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Air particles oscillate locally; the compression/rarefaction disturbance travels through successive interactions.

attempt.produces: One particle-motion statement and one propagation statement.

rubric.criterion: Particle motion is local and mainly parallel to propagation.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing the longitudinal nature of the fluid sound wave.

rubric.criterion: The disturbance propagates farther than any one particle.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating medium motion from wave motion.

accepted: Particle oscillates left-right near equilibrium while compression pattern travels right.
rejected: The marked particle rides with the wave all the way to the listener.

route.ask: What direction does the wave travel?
route.why_this_ask: It fixes the propagation axis.

route.ask: Along what direction do nearby particles move?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies longitudinal local motion.

route.ask: What happens to one marked particle after the compression passes?
route.why_this_ask: It separates local oscillation from propagation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path constructs compression/rarefaction from particle motion; the learner route starts from the travelling pulse and traces one particle backward.

boundary_test.prompt: If all particles were permanently carried from source to listener by each sound pulse, would the medium remain approximately in place after repeated sound?
boundary_test.answer: No; that would imply sustained bulk transport inconsistent with the local-oscillation model.
boundary_test.confirms: Sound propagation is not ordinary mass transport across the whole path.

microtopics.title: Sound graphs separate amplitude, wavelength, period, frequency and speed
microtopics.badge_reason: Frequency, wavelength and amplitude can all change independently enough that verbal mixing is common.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish the wave pattern from local particle motion and can read labelled graph axes.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A spatial graph gives wavelength from repeat distance, a temporal graph gives period from repeat time, amplitude comes from vertical extent, f=1/T, and for one wave in one medium/state v=fλ; changing medium can change v.

teaching_path.action: Compare the sampled spatial snapshot with the sampled time trace and read each horizontal-axis label before naming a repeat interval.
teaching_path.why_valid: Repeat distance on a position axis is wavelength, while repeat time on a time axis is period; the axis determines the physical meaning.
teaching_path.output: spatial repeat: lambda = 1.7 m; temporal repeat: T = 0.005 s; vertical amplitude = 1 cm.

teaching_path.action: Take the reciprocal of the positive period read from the temporal graph.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-FREQUENCY-PERIOD owns the conversion from time per cycle to cycles per second.

teaching_path.action: Follow one repeated phase: in one period T the travelling pattern advances one wavelength lambda, then replace 1/T with f.
teaching_path.why_valid: Speed is distance per time for the same pattern, and the gate-owned relations bind T and f for the same wave.
teaching_path.output: v = lambda/T = f lambda = 200 Hz × 1.7 m = 340 m/s.

teaching_path.action: Change only the plotted vertical amplitude while holding repeat spacing fixed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Amplitude measures disturbance size, whereas period/frequency and wavelength measure repeat spacing on different axes.
teaching_path.output: amplitude can change from 1 cm to 2 cm while T = 0.005 s, f = 200 Hz, and lambda = 1.7 m remain unchanged.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A taller wave automatically has a higher frequency.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two traces have the same horizontal repeat time but different vertical amplitudes. Must their frequencies differ?
misconceptions.repair: Read the horizontal time spacing for period/frequency; amplitude comes from vertical extent.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The same frequency and wavelength values can be mixed across different media to infer one universal sound speed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A sound enters a different medium. Can you keep the old wavelength and the new frequency in v=fλ without checking that they describe the same wave state?
misconceptions.repair: Use f and λ from the same wave/medium state. Medium change can change propagation speed and wavelength.

exit_task.prompt: A spatial sound graph has adjacent positive peaks 1.7 m apart, and a time trace of the same wave at one location has adjacent positive peaks 0.005 s apart. The vertical amplitude is 1 cm. Identify wavelength, period and amplitude, then find frequency and wave speed.

answer.summary: lambda = 1.7 m, T = 0.005 s, amplitude = 1 cm, f = 200 Hz, and v = 340 m/s.
reasoning: The spatial repeat distance gives wavelength: lambda = 1.7 m.
The temporal repeat interval gives period: T = 0.005 s.
The vertical extreme gives amplitude: 1 cm.
One wavelength advances in one period, so v = lambda/T = f lambda = 340 m/s.
answer.check: The units confirm Hz × m = m/s, and changing amplitude alone would not alter the repeat spacings.

microtopics.research_contribution: Local Grade9V3 wave-quantity construction enriched from prior acoustics engineering with explicit same-wave/same-medium validity checks.

predict.prompt: In the same medium, if sound frequency doubles while propagation speed stays the same, what must happen to wavelength?
predict.defensible_answer: Wavelength halves because v = f lambda.

attempt.produces: A period-to-frequency conversion and a same-wave speed calculation.

rubric.criterion: Uses reciprocal period for frequency.
rubric.evidence_of: Distinguishing time per cycle from cycles per second.

rubric.criterion: Pairs frequency and wavelength from the same wave.
rubric.evidence_of: Applying v = f lambda without mixing data.

rejected: f = T or v = f/lambda.

route.ask: Is 0.005 s a count per second or time per cycle?
route.why_this_ask: It distinguishes T from f.

route.ask: What reciprocal converts time per cycle to cycles per second?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs f=1/T.

route.ask: Which spatial quantity pairs with that frequency?
route.why_this_ask: It introduces wavelength.

route.ask: If medium speed stays fixed, how must f and lambda co-vary?
route.why_this_ask: It independently checks the relation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path labels the quantities first; the learner route starts from the units of period and reconstructs the reciprocal and product relations.

boundary_test.prompt: Can amplitude change while frequency and wavelength remain unchanged?
boundary_test.answer: Yes, within the simple wave description.
boundary_test.confirms: Amplitude is a separate disturbance-size quantity rather than another name for frequency or wavelength.

microtopics.title: Pitch, loudness and the approximate human audible range are different questions
microtopics.badge_reason: Pitch and loudness are everyday words that learners often swap with frequency and amplitude.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish frequency from amplitude and can compare two wave descriptions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Frequency controls pitch for heard tones, sound strength/intensity is a different loudness dimension, and humans usually hear only a finite frequency band—approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz for typical young hearing—whose limits vary between people and with age.

teaching_path.action: Compare two waves with different frequencies but matched amplitudes.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding disturbance size fixed isolates repetition rate as the changed feature.
teaching_path.output: higher f -> higher pitch under comparable conditions.

teaching_path.action: Compare two waves with different amplitudes/intensities but the same frequency.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding repetition rate fixed isolates loudness-related strength from pitch.
teaching_path.output: greater sound intensity / typically larger amplitude -> louder percept, while pitch stays tied to f.

teaching_path.action: Change frequency and amplitude in opposite directions and require two separate predictions.
teaching_path.why_valid: The mixed case tests whether pitch and loudness have been collapsed into one idea.
teaching_path.output: pitch prediction from f; loudness prediction from sound strength/intensity information.

teaching_path.action: Compare example frequencies with the approximate usual human audible band from the scientific-check source.
teaching_path.why_valid: The current curriculum asks learners to explain audible range, while the separate source supplies the approximate numerical bounds rather than the curriculum mapping inventing them.
teaching_path.output: usual human audible band ≈ 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; 10 Hz lies below it, 1,000 Hz lies within it, and 25,000 Hz lies above it.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A louder sound must have a higher pitch.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can a low-pitched drum sound be louder than a high-pitched whistle?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Use frequency for pitch and sound strength/intensity for loudness; they are separate dimensions.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The 20 Hz and 20,000 Hz figures are exact universal hearing cutoffs for every person.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Would every person of every age necessarily hear a 19,999 Hz tone but fail to hear a 20,001 Hz tone?
misconceptions.repair: No. Treat 20 Hz–20 kHz as an approximate usual range; individual hearing limits vary, especially with age and hearing condition.

exit_task.prompt: Classify 10 Hz, 1,000 Hz and 25,000 Hz relative to the approximate usual human audible range, then state which physical quantity mainly tracks pitch for an audible tone.

answer.summary: 10 Hz is below the usual audible band, 1,000 Hz is within it, and 25,000 Hz is above it. For audible tones, higher frequency corresponds to higher pitch under comparable conditions.
reasoning: The approximate usual human range is about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
10 Hz is below the lower bound; 1,000 Hz lies between the bounds; 25,000 Hz is above the upper bound.
Pitch comparisons use frequency, not amplitude or loudness.
answer.check: The range is approximate and varies among people; the classification is a Grade 9 model, not a personal hearing diagnosis.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The numerical boundary values are source-backed classification thresholds rather than a computed formula claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created pitch/loudness/audible-range distinction; approximate numerical hearing bounds are held by a separate CBSE scientific-check resource.

predict.prompt: Must a higher-pitched sound also be louder?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Pitch follows frequency; loudness depends on sound strength/intensity and can vary independently.

attempt.produces: Separate pitch and loudness predictions for a mixed comparison.

rubric.criterion: Uses frequency only for the pitch comparison.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping repetition rate tied to pitch.

rubric.criterion: Uses sound strength/intensity information for loudness.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating loudness from frequency.

accepted: Higher frequency -> higher pitch; larger amplitude/intensity can make the other sound louder.
rejected: Higher frequency automatically means louder.

route.ask: Which measured quantity counts cycles per second?
route.why_this_ask: It recovers frequency.

route.ask: Which percept changes with frequency?
route.why_this_ask: It maps f to pitch.

route.ask: Which comparison is about sound strength rather than repetition rate?
route.why_this_ask: It separates loudness.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path uses controlled comparisons; the learner route starts from the everyday words and maps each back to the physical quantity.

boundary_test.answer: No. It is a usual approximate range; individual limits vary.
boundary_test.confirms: The curriculum model is not being misrepresented as a universal biological cutoff.

microtopics.title: Reflected sound can form echoes, reverberation and echolocation cues
microtopics.badge_reason: The common arithmetic error is forgetting the round trip; a second modeling error is treating one memorized delay/distance threshold as universally defining an echo.
entry_assumptions: Can use wave speed and elapsed time and can distinguish one-way from round-trip travel.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Reflected-sound timing measures an outward-and-return path. One-way range is half that path for a stationary simple geometry; whether a return is heard as a distinct echo versus reverberation depends on delay/conditions rather than one universal distance constant.

teaching_path.action: Trace the sound path from source to reflector and back to the receiver before writing a timing relation.
teaching_path.why_valid: The measured echo delay covers both outward and return legs.
teaching_path.output: total reflected path = outward leg + return leg

teaching_path.action: For a stationary reflector and one clear round-trip delay in the same medium, use d = v t_echo / 2.
teaching_path.why_valid: v times the full delay gives the total path length; the one-way range is half that in the simple geometry.
teaching_path.output: one-way reflector distance = v t_echo / 2

teaching_path.action: Classify clearly separated returns as echo-like and densely overlapping returns as reverberation, while treating the perceptual boundary as condition-dependent.
teaching_path.why_valid: Echo and reverberation are distinguished by temporal separation/overlap of reflected sound, not by one universal wall distance.
teaching_path.output: distinct return vs overlapping reflected sound

teaching_path.action: Use echolocation/ranging as a transfer case: emitted sound plus measured return delay provides a range cue only after the round-trip path is recognized.
teaching_path.why_valid: The factor-of-two geometry is the reusable invariant across simple echo-ranging contexts.
teaching_path.output: known v + round-trip delay -> range cue

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Echo delay time corresponds to one-way travel from source to wall.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A clap returns after 0.4 s. Did the sound spend all 0.4 s travelling only outward?
misconceptions.repair: No. The delay includes outward and return travel, so v t is the round-trip path and one-way range is half.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A single memorized reflector distance universally decides whether any reflected sound is heard as a separate echo.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If sound speed, listener/source geometry or perceptual conditions change, must one memorized wall distance still be the universal echo boundary?
misconceptions.repair: Use the actual reflection delay and conditions. The simple calculation concerns round-trip timing; a distinct-echo threshold is not a universal geometry constant.

exit_task.prompt: Sound travels at 340 m/s and a clear echo returns 0.40 s after a clap from a stationary wall. Estimate the one-way distance to the wall.

answer.summary: The wall is about 68 m away.
reasoning: The 0.40 s is a round-trip delay.
Total sound path = 340 x 0.40 = 136 m.
One-way distance = 136/2 = 68 m.
answer.check: Doubling the wall distance at the same sound speed would double the echo delay.

microtopics.research_contribution: Copied and adapted from prior acoustics engineering for the round-trip invariant; donor-specific universal echo-threshold wording was deliberately not copied.

predict.prompt: If a wall is twice as far away and sound speed is unchanged, what happens to the echo delay?
predict.defensible_answer: It doubles because both the outward and return path lengths double.

attempt.produces: A round-trip path statement, one echo-distance calculation, and an echo-versus-reverberation classification.

rubric.criterion: Uses half the round-trip path for one-way distance.
rubric.evidence_of: Accounting for outward and reflected travel.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes separate echo from overlapping reverberation.
rubric.evidence_of: Using delay structure rather than treating all reflection effects as identical.

accepted: 340 m/s x 0.40 s / 2 = 68 m; distinct delayed return = echo.
rejected: 340 x 0.40 = 136 m as the one-way wall distance.

route.ask: Where does the sound travel before you hear the return?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes both legs.

route.ask: What distance does v times the whole delay represent?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies total round-trip path.

route.ask: How do you recover one-way range?
route.why_this_ask: It reconstructs the factor one half.

route.ask: When do multiple returns merge into a prolonged sound instead of a separate echo?
route.why_this_ask: It distinguishes reverberation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path lays out reflection categories; the learner route starts from the timing calculation and reconstructs the physical path.

boundary_test.prompt: If echo delay is zero in this simple stationary-path model, what one-way distance does the relation return?
boundary_test.answer: Zero.
boundary_test.confirms: The factor-of-two relation is tied to a nonnegative round-trip path.

relations.meaning: For a repeating vibration, frequency is the reciprocal of time period.
conditions: f and T refer to the same repeating vibration.

derivation.action: Take the reciprocal of the positive time per cycle.
derivation.why_valid: Frequency counts cycles per second while period measures seconds per cycle.

limits: The relation assumes a repeating vibration with a meaningful period.
checks: f T = 1.
Longer period means lower frequency.

relations.meaning: Wave propagation speed equals temporal frequency times spatial wavelength.
conditions: f >= 0 and lambda >= 0.
All quantities describe the same wave mode in the same medium/state.

derivation.action: Follow one identifiable phase of the travelling pattern through one complete cycle.
derivation.why_valid: During one period T, the repeating pattern advances by one wavelength lambda.
derivation.output: distance advanced in one cycle = lambda; elapsed time for that cycle = T.

derivation.action: Divide the one-cycle advance by the one-cycle time, then replace 1/T with frequency.
derivation.why_valid: Speed is distance per time and REL-FREQUENCY-PERIOD gives f = 1/T for the same repeating wave.

limits: Changing medium can change propagation speed; do not assume one speed across different media.
checks: Hz times m gives m/s.
At fixed medium speed, increasing f requires decreasing lambda.

relations.meaning: For a single echo from a stationary reflecting surface, one-way source-to-reflector distance is half the sound speed times the measured round-trip echo delay.
conditions: t_echo >= 0.
The measured delay is for one outward-and-return path in the same medium.

derivation.action: Write total reflected path as twice the one-way range for a source/receiver at the same location.
derivation.why_valid: The sound travels to the reflector and back.

derivation.action: Set total path equal to v t_echo and solve for d.
derivation.why_valid: Distance travelled equals wave speed times elapsed time in the stated uniform-medium model.

limits: Moving source/reflector geometry or multiple ambiguous reflections need a richer model.
checks: Doubling d doubles t_echo at fixed v.
The factor one half prevents round-trip distance from being mistaken for one-way range.

questions.stem: A spatial sound graph has adjacent positive peaks 1.7 m apart, and a time trace of the same wave at one location has adjacent positive peaks 0.005 s apart. The vertical amplitude is 1 cm. Identify wavelength, period and amplitude, then find frequency and wave speed.

answer.summary: lambda = 1.7 m, T = 0.005 s, amplitude = 1 cm, f = 200 Hz, and v = 340 m/s.
reasoning: The spatial repeat distance gives wavelength: lambda = 1.7 m.
The temporal repeat interval gives period: T = 0.005 s.
The vertical extreme gives amplitude: 1 cm.
One wavelength advances in one period, so v = lambda/T = f lambda = 340 m/s.

reasoning: The source vibration can remain.

Removing the gas removes that propagation path.

questions.stem: Design an experiment to determine the speed of one pulse along a stretched string or slinky. State the measured path length and time, the speed calculation, and how you would reduce timing error.

answer.summary: Measure a known propagation distance L along the stretched medium and the travel time Delta t for the pulse over that path, calculate v = L/Delta t, repeat several trials under the same tension, and average or use a longer timed path to reduce reaction-time error.
reasoning: Mark a known propagation distance along the stretched string/slinky.
Generate a clear pulse and measure the time for the same identifiable pulse feature to travel between the marks.
Calculate pulse speed from travelled path divided by elapsed time.
Keep tension and medium setup fixed during repeated trials.
Repeat measurements or increase the timed path to reduce the relative effect of start/stop timing uncertainty.

buckets.title: Oscillation foundation: stable equilibrium
buckets.badge_reason: The entry distinction separates return-directed behavior from mere repetition before quantitative oscillator models are used.

capabilities.action: Identify whether a displaced system has a tendency directed back toward one stable equilibrium.
capabilities.success_criterion: Classify a repeated motion by whether displacement to either side produces a return-directed tendency.

capabilities.action: Track how kinetic and potential energy trade through one ideal oscillation cycle while total mechanical energy stays fixed.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify the two kinetic-energy maxima in one displacement cycle and explain why opposite equal displacements carry the same potential-energy state.

microtopics.title: Repetition is not enough: look for a stable equilibrium
microtopics.badge_reason: Repeated motion is visually salient, so learners can miss the stronger requirement that the system's response be organized around one stable equilibrium.
entry_assumptions: Can identify a repeated back-and-forth motion and distinguish position from direction of motion.
microtopics.inferential_jump: An oscillation is organized around a stable equilibrium: when displaced, the system has a tendency that points back toward that equilibrium.

teaching_path.action: Mark one position as the equilibrium and label displacements on opposite sides of it.
teaching_path.why_valid: A return tendency can only be judged relative to a named equilibrium; otherwise back has no fixed destination.
teaching_path.output: left displacement | equilibrium | right displacement

teaching_path.action: Move the same system first to the left of equilibrium and then to the right, recording the direction of its tendency each time.
teaching_path.why_valid: If the equilibrium is stable, the direction must reverse when the side of displacement reverses so that it points inward in both cases.
teaching_path.output: left side -> tendency right; right side -> tendency left

teaching_path.action: Compare that pattern with a motion that repeats around a circular track but has no single position toward which displacement produces a return tendency.
teaching_path.why_valid: The counterexample keeps repetition while removing the stable-equilibrium structure, showing that repetition alone is insufficient.
teaching_path.output: repeats -> yes; one return-directed equilibrium -> no

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any motion that repeats is automatically simple harmonic motion.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ball moves periodically around a circular track. Does repetition alone show a restoring tendency toward one equilibrium position?
misconceptions.repair: Separate periodicity from the restoring condition; repetition by itself does not identify simple harmonic motion.

exit_task.prompt: Three motions repeat. For each, decide whether one stable equilibrium organizes the motion and justify the choice by what happens after a displacement to either side.

answer.summary: A qualifying motion has one equilibrium toward which the system tends to return from either side; repetition without that inward pattern is not enough.
reasoning: Name the candidate equilibrium before judging the motion.
Check the response after a displacement on one side and then the other side.
Accept the classification only when the response reverses so that it points toward the same equilibrium from both sides.
answer.check: Swap the side of displacement. A stable equilibrium should make the return tendency swap direction as well; a merely repeating path need not.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is a qualitative classification of restoring behavior and makes no computed period, frequency or amplitude claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created counterexample sequence isolates stable-equilibrium reasoning before any later oscillator equation is admitted.

predict.prompt: If a motion repeats perfectly, is that alone enough to show it is organized around a stable equilibrium?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Repetition can occur without a single position that produces an inward return tendency from both sides.

attempt.produces: A marked equilibrium for each candidate motion, with arrows showing the response after equal displacements to opposite sides.

rubric.criterion: One equilibrium candidate is explicitly marked before arrows are judged.
rubric.evidence_of: Making the reference position part of the reasoning.

rubric.criterion: The response direction is tested on both sides rather than inferred from one example.
rubric.evidence_of: Showing the inward pattern that defines the distinction.

accepted: The sketch marks one center and shows left displacement returning right and right displacement returning left, while the repeating circular case is rejected for lacking that one-center pattern.
rejected: The response accepts every repeating path and never checks what a displacement to the opposite side would make the system do.

route.ask: Where would you place one position that the system could be displaced away from?
route.why_this_ask: A return tendency is meaningless until the learner proposes an equilibrium.

route.ask: After moving the system to the left of that point, which way would a return tendency have to point?
route.why_this_ask: The first side gives a concrete directional prediction.

route.ask: Now move it to the other side. What must reverse if the same point is truly stable?
route.why_this_ask: The second side tests whether the result is structural rather than accidental.

route.ask: Can a circular repeating path pass the same two-sided test?
route.why_this_ask: The counterexample removes stable equilibrium while preserving repetition.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path contrasts examples directly; the elicitation route makes the learner nominate an equilibrium and commit to two opposite-side predictions before seeing the counterexample.

boundary_test.prompt: If the system is placed exactly at the stable equilibrium and left undisturbed, which return direction should be preferred?
boundary_test.answer: Neither side should be preferred; the defining return-direction test begins after a displacement away from equilibrium.
boundary_test.confirms: The concept concerns response to displacement around an equilibrium, not a permanent arrow attached at the center.

microtopics.title: Energy trades twice during one displacement cycle
microtopics.badge_reason: The position cycle repeats once while the energy pattern repeats at both center crossings, so learners must coordinate two time patterns without confusing sign with stored energy.
entry_assumptions: Can identify turning points and equilibrium crossings in a repeated back-and-forth motion.
Can read a quantity as nonnegative even when position lies on the negative side of equilibrium.
microtopics.inferential_jump: In an ideal oscillator, energy shifts between motion and displacement storage while the total stays fixed; the energy state is the same at equal-magnitude displacements on opposite sides, so the kinetic-potential pattern repeats twice during one full displacement cycle.

teaching_path.action: Mark five ordered checkpoints for one full displacement cycle: positive turning point, center crossing, negative turning point, second center crossing, and return to the positive turning point.
teaching_path.why_valid: The energy pattern can only be counted against a complete position cycle if the cycle's repeated geometric checkpoints are fixed first.
teaching_path.output: +turn -> center -> -turn -> center -> +turn

teaching_path.action: Assign the dominant energy form at each checkpoint while keeping the same total mechanical-energy level across the row.
teaching_path.why_valid: At turning points the instantaneous motion is absent while displacement storage is greatest; at center crossings the displacement storage is least while motion is greatest.
teaching_path.output: turn: KE low / PE high ; center: KE high / PE low ; turn: KE low / PE high ; center: KE high / PE low

teaching_path.action: Compare the positive and negative turning points, then count the center crossings before the displacement pattern returns to its start.
teaching_path.why_valid: Opposite equal-magnitude displacements produce the same energy state, so sign reversal does not make stored energy negative; two center crossings give two kinetic-energy maxima per position cycle.
teaching_path.output: +turn energy state = -turn energy state ; 1 displacement cycle -> 2 KE maxima

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Potential energy becomes negative whenever displacement is on the negative side of equilibrium.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At equal distances on opposite sides of equilibrium, should the ideal oscillator have different stored-energy amounts just because one position has a negative sign?
misconceptions.repair: Treat the side of equilibrium and the stored-energy amount separately: opposite equal-magnitude displacements have the same potential-energy state.

exit_task.prompt: Follow one ideal oscillation from a positive turning point back to the same turning point. How many times does kinetic energy reach a maximum, and why does the total mechanical energy not rise and fall with those maxima?

answer.summary: Kinetic energy reaches a maximum twice, once at each equilibrium crossing, while the total mechanical energy stays constant because kinetic and potential energy exchange rather than being created or destroyed.
reasoning: One full displacement cycle crosses equilibrium twice before returning to the starting turning point.
Each center crossing is the state of greatest motion and least displacement storage, so kinetic energy peaks at both crossings.
At the turning points the balance reverses; the changing shares add to the same total throughout the ideal cycle.
answer.check: Lay the energy sequence under the five position checkpoints; the first and last energy states must match, and the two center checkpoints must carry the two kinetic-energy maxima.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer gives a qualitative cycle count and conservation explanation; it computes no energy value, frequency, or oscillator parameter.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created checkpoint sequence teaches the double-repeat energy pattern and sign-independent stored-energy distinction without introducing an ungated oscillator energy equation.

predict.prompt: During one complete back-and-forth position cycle, do you expect kinetic energy to peak once or more than once?
predict.defensible_answer: It peaks twice, because the oscillator passes through equilibrium twice before returning to the starting turning point.

attempt.produces: A five-checkpoint position row with kinetic and potential energy marked high or low at each checkpoint and one constant-total line beneath it.

rubric.criterion: Both equilibrium crossings are marked as kinetic-energy maxima.
rubric.evidence_of: Coordinating the energy pattern with the full displacement cycle rather than counting only half a cycle.

rubric.criterion: Opposite turning points are assigned the same stored-energy state and the total is kept fixed.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating position sign from energy sign and applying ideal mechanical-energy conservation.

accepted: The row shows high kinetic energy at both center crossings, high potential energy at both turning points, and one unchanged total across all five checkpoints.
rejected: The negative turning point is assigned negative potential energy and only one center crossing is counted before the cycle is declared complete.

route.ask: What ordered checkpoints must you pass before the displacement pattern has truly returned to its starting state?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must define a complete cycle before counting energy events.

route.ask: At a turning point, which energy share is largest and which is smallest?
route.why_this_ask: This anchors the energy bookkeeping at a state with no instantaneous motion.

route.ask: How many center crossings occur before the position cycle closes, and what energy event occurs at each?
route.why_this_ask: This produces the twice-per-cycle pattern from the motion rather than stating it.

route.ask: Why should the two opposite turning points have the same stored-energy state?
route.why_this_ask: The final ask directly tests the misconception that negative position implies negative stored energy.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path lays out the five checkpoints before assigning energy; the elicitation route makes the learner define the cycle boundary and discover the repeated energy state by counting crossings.

boundary_test.prompt: If mechanical energy is lost to an external dissipative interaction, should the constant-total row still be used unchanged?
boundary_test.answer: No. The constant-total claim belongs to the ideal oscillator case; with an energy-losing interaction the mechanical total can decrease.
boundary_test.confirms: The conservation statement is tied to the ideal model rather than asserted for every real oscillation.

microtopics.title: Mass distribution sets rotational inertia about an axis
microtopics.badge_reason: The comparison is qualitative but only works if the axis stays explicit while the mass distribution changes.
entry_assumptions: Can compare distances from a line or point and can describe rigid rotation about a chosen axis.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Rotational inertia depends on how mass is distributed relative to the chosen axis, not on total mass alone.

teaching_path.action: Lay out two equal totals of identical mass pieces around one named axis: one cluster close to the axis and one spread farther away.
teaching_path.why_valid: The totals match and the axis is unchanged, so radial distribution is the only intended difference.
teaching_path.output: same total mass | same axis | arrangement A: pieces near | arrangement B: pieces far

teaching_path.action: Move the pieces of arrangement A outward without adding or removing any mass, then compare how the rotational response changes.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only the distances from the fixed axis were changed, isolating the effect of radial placement.
teaching_path.output: near placement -> farther placement; total mass = unchanged; rotational inertia -> larger

teaching_path.action: Compare a rim-loaded body with a centre-loaded body that has the same total mass and outer size.
teaching_path.why_valid: If total mass alone controlled the comparison the two would match; the different distribution supplies the discriminating case.
teaching_path.output: equal total mass + equal outer size; more mass farther from axis -> greater rotational inertia

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Objects with the same mass always have the same moment of inertia.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ring and a solid disk have the same mass and radius about the same central axis. Must their moments of inertia be equal?
misconceptions.repair: Track how much mass lies far from the axis; the squared distance weighting makes distribution matter.

exit_task.prompt: Two equal-mass arrangements rotate about the same marked axis. One keeps most of its mass close to the axis; the other places more mass near the outside. Predict which has greater rotational inertia and name the feature that decides it.

answer.summary: The outside-loaded arrangement has greater rotational inertia because more of the same mass lies farther from the chosen axis.
reasoning: The comparison fixes total mass, so mass amount cannot explain the difference.
The comparison fixes the axis, so the reference for all distances is common.
Moving the same mass farther from that axis increases its contribution to rotational inertia.
answer.check: Swap only the radial distributions while keeping the axis fixed; the prediction must swap with the distribution rather than stay attached to an object label.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer makes a qualitative ordering only; it contains no computed value or asserted numerical magnitude.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created conceptual rung derived from the matrix distinction. The imported packet was consulted only as non-authoritative input; scientific and pedagogical review are still required.

predict.prompt: Two bodies have the same total mass and outer size, but one carries more mass near the outside. Must they be equally hard to change in rotation about the same axis?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The body with more mass farther from the axis has greater rotational inertia.

attempt.produces: A side-by-side sketch that keeps the same axis and total mass while relocating the mass pieces radially.

rubric.criterion: The same axis is marked in both arrangements.
rubric.evidence_of: The comparison is about distribution relative to one reference axis.

rubric.criterion: The mass pieces are redistributed without changing their total.
rubric.evidence_of: Total mass is held fixed while radial placement is isolated.

accepted: Both sketches show the same axis and same number of equal pieces, with one set visibly farther from the axis; the explanation ties the ordering to radial placement.
rejected: The second sketch adds more pieces or changes the axis, so the comparison cannot distinguish distribution from total mass or reference choice.

route.ask: What must stay fixed if you want to test whether distribution matters rather than total mass?
route.why_this_ask: It forces the comparison to isolate one variable before any conclusion is offered.

route.ask: If no mass is added, what single change can make the two arrangements different?
route.why_this_ask: It directs attention to distance from the common axis.

route.ask: Which arrangement places more of the same mass farther from the axis?
route.why_this_ask: The learner identifies the physically relevant distribution instead of recalling a named object.

route.ask: What prediction follows if radial placement, not total mass, is the deciding feature?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the learner state the inferential jump after constructing the controlled comparison.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path supplies a controlled redistribution and its comparison; the learner route first chooses what must be held fixed, then constructs the comparison before naming the deciding feature.

boundary_test.prompt: If every mass piece is moved to the same radial distance in both arrangements while total mass and axis remain fixed, should the distribution-based difference remain?
boundary_test.answer: No. Once the radial distributions match, this particular reason for different rotational inertia disappears.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner attributes the difference to radial distribution about the stated axis rather than to an object name.

microtopics.title: Angular momentum conservation belongs to a specified origin
microtopics.badge_reason: The central difficulty is keeping the turning-effect test and angular-momentum statement tied to the same origin while the body's distribution changes.
entry_assumptions: Can identify an origin used for a turning-effect statement.
Can describe an axial direction for rotational quantities without changing the physical plane.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Angular momentum and torque must be taken about the same specified origin; zero net external torque about that origin makes total angular momentum there constant.

teaching_path.action: Mark one origin O and write it beside both the external turning-effect check and the angular-momentum description.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing the reference point can change the turning effect, so the conservation claim is meaningful only when both quantities use the same origin.
teaching_path.output: origin for external turning effect: O | origin for angular momentum: O

teaching_path.action: Move part of a rotating system inward while keeping the stated external turning effect about O absent.
teaching_path.why_valid: With the reference origin fixed and no external turning effect about it, the system can redistribute internally without changing total angular momentum about O.
teaching_path.output: mass distribution: outward -> inward; external turning effect about O = none; spin rate -> increases

teaching_path.action: Choose a different point P that the same external force does not pass through and ask whether the earlier conservation statement automatically transfers to P.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same force can have no turning effect about O but a nonzero one about P, exposing why origin matching is a condition rather than a label.
teaching_path.output: about O: external turning effect absent | about P: external turning effect present -> conservation claim must be rechecked

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a system is isolated from external forces, angular momentum is automatically conserved about every origin.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A force passes through one origin but not another. Is angular momentum conserved about both origins?
misconceptions.repair: Test external torque about the same origin used for angular momentum; force isolation alone is not the criterion.

exit_task.prompt: A rotating system pulls mass inward. The problem states that the net external turning effect about origin O is zero. Predict the spin-rate change and explain why the conservation claim must stay tied to O.

answer.summary: The spin rate rises as the mass distribution moves inward, while total angular momentum about O remains constant under the stated zero-external-torque condition there.
reasoning: The reference origin is fixed as O for both the condition and the conserved quantity.
Moving mass inward changes how the rotating mass is distributed about O.
With no net external turning effect about O, the redistribution changes spin rate rather than total angular momentum about O.
answer.check: Repeat the reasoning after naming another origin; if an external turning effect exists there, the conservation claim must be reconsidered instead of copied.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response predicts directions of change and a conservation condition without claiming a calculated angular momentum or angular speed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created origin-discipline rung. It intentionally does not author the missing quantitative torque relation from R2 and therefore treats that prior rung as an explicit conceptual dependency gap.

predict.prompt: A force line passes through origin O but misses point P. Can one angular-momentum conservation statement be copied unchanged from O to P?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The external turning effect must be checked about the same origin used for angular momentum; the answer can differ between O and P.

attempt.produces: A two-origin diagram showing the same force line together with a separate conservation decision for O and for P.

rubric.criterion: The same physical force is shown relative to both origins.
rubric.evidence_of: The changed conclusion comes from reference choice rather than from changing the interaction.

rubric.criterion: Each conservation statement names its own origin.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner keeps the condition and conserved quantity paired to one reference point.

accepted: The force line passes through O but not P, with the note 'check about O' kept separate from 'check about P'; the response refuses to transfer the conclusion automatically.
rejected: The response writes 'angular momentum conserved' once with no origin, which hides the condition the rung is meant to establish.

route.ask: Which point is being used to judge the external turning effect?
route.why_this_ask: It makes the reference explicit before any conservation language appears.

route.ask: If the same system pulls mass inward with that condition unchanged, what changes visibly?
route.why_this_ask: It separates redistribution from loss of the conserved quantity.

route.ask: Does the force line have the same relation to a second point P?
route.why_this_ask: It creates the counterexample that makes the origin condition necessary.

route.ask: What must be named every time you claim conservation here?
route.why_this_ask: The learner states the origin-matching rule rather than merely accepting the example.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path states one origin, changes the distribution, then probes a second origin; the elicitation instead begins by withholding the conservation verdict and makes the learner decide separately for each reference point.

boundary_test.prompt: If the net external turning effect is zero about both O and P for a particular isolated system, may conservation be stated about both?
boundary_test.answer: Yes, but as two separately justified statements, each tied to the origin for which the zero-turning-effect condition has been checked.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner understands that the origin condition is local to the conservation statement rather than an arbitrary notation choice.

microtopics.title: Pure rolling makes the contact point instantaneously at rest
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must combine translation with rotation at different points of one rigid body without treating every point as having the centre speed.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish centre-of-mass translation from rotation about the centre.
Can add two directed velocity contributions qualitatively.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Pure rolling couples translation and rotation so that the point touching a stationary surface is instantaneously at rest relative to that surface.

teaching_path.action: Draw a wheel moving right and mark three points: top, centre, and the point touching the stationary ground.
teaching_path.why_valid: The rigid body is one object, but the three points occupy different places relative to the centre and therefore need not share one ground-frame velocity.
teaching_path.output: marked points: top | centre | contact; ground: stationary

teaching_path.action: At each marked point, place the rightward translation contribution beside the rotational contribution from turning about the centre.
teaching_path.why_valid: Ground-frame motion of a point on a rolling rigid body is obtained by combining the motion of the centre with motion about the centre.
teaching_path.output: contact: rightward + leftward -> rest | centre: rightward + none -> rightward | top: rightward + rightward -> faster rightward

teaching_path.action: Ask what would be observed at the contact point if the wheel were sliding instead of rolling purely.
teaching_path.why_valid: A nonzero ground-frame contact speed is the discriminating boundary: cancellation at contact is the defining no-slip feature used here.
teaching_path.output: pure rolling -> contact instantaneously at rest | sliding -> contact has nonzero ground-frame motion

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every point on a rolling wheel moves forward with the centre-of-mass speed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: For a wheel rolling right without slipping, what is the instantaneous velocity of the point touching the ground?
misconceptions.repair: Add translational and rotational velocity contributions; at the contact point they cancel for pure rolling.

exit_task.prompt: A wheel rolls right on stationary ground without slipping. Rank the instantaneous ground-frame motions of the top, centre, and contact point, and explain why the contact point is special.

answer.summary: The contact point is instantaneously at rest, the centre moves forward, and the top moves forward faster than the centre because translation and rotation combine differently at those locations.
reasoning: Every point shares the centre's translational motion.
Rotation about the centre contributes different directions at the top and contact.
At contact the two contributions oppose and cancel in pure rolling; at the top they reinforce.
answer.check: Change only the condition from pure rolling to sliding; the contact-point cancellation should no longer be asserted.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The model answer compares qualitative point motions and asserts no computed speed.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created kinematic rolling rung. It uses no rolling-energy equation and no quantitative no-slip formula; the contact-point condition is taught through velocity composition.

predict.prompt: A wheel rolls right without slipping. Is the point touching the ground moving right at the same instant?
predict.defensible_answer: No. In the ground frame that contact point is instantaneously at rest even though the wheel's centre is moving right.

attempt.produces: A three-point velocity sketch for the top, centre, and contact point with translation and rotation contributions shown separately.

rubric.criterion: The contact point receives opposite translation and rotation contributions.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner constructs the no-slip cancellation rather than memorizing a point-speed list.

rubric.criterion: The top point receives reinforcing forward contributions.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner applies the same composition rule consistently around the wheel.

accepted: The sketch shows cancellation at contact, one forward contribution at the centre, and reinforcement at the top, with the ground explicitly stationary.
rejected: All three points are assigned the same forward arrow because the body is rigid; rigidity constrains distances, not equality of ground-frame velocities.

route.ask: Which motion contribution is shared by every point because the centre is translating?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the common part before adding the location-dependent part.

route.ask: At the bottom point, which way does rotation about the centre move that point relative to the centre?
route.why_this_ask: The bottom contribution is the one needed to expose cancellation.

route.ask: What ground-frame motion remains when the two contact-point contributions are combined?
route.why_this_ask: The learner performs the decisive composition instead of receiving the result.

route.ask: What changes first if the wheel begins to slide?
route.why_this_ask: It checks that zero contact motion is tied to the no-slip condition rather than to wheels in general.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative route labels all three point motions before testing sliding; the elicitation withholds the contact result and makes the learner construct it from two directional contributions.

boundary_test.prompt: A locked wheel skids right without turning. Is the point touching the ground instantaneously at rest?
boundary_test.answer: No. Without the rotational contribution that cancels translation in pure rolling, the contact point slides right relative to the ground.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner associates instantaneous contact rest with the no-slip composition rather than with mere contact between wheel and ground.

microtopics.title: Mass distribution changes ideal rolling acceleration
microtopics.badge_reason: The comparison is conceptual only if mass amount, radius, incline, and no-slip conditions are controlled while shape changes.
entry_assumptions: Can separate translational motion from rotation in pure rolling.
Can reason that one energy input may be divided among different motion channels.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For bodies rolling without slipping, how mass is distributed relative to size controls how gravitational energy divides between translation and rotation, so total mass alone does not decide which body accelerates more.

teaching_path.action: Release two equal-mass, equal-radius bodies from the same marked height on the same incline, differing only in how their mass is distributed.
teaching_path.why_valid: Holding mass, size, release height, and incline fixed makes distribution the intended cause of any difference in motion.
teaching_path.output: same mass | same radius | same start height | distribution A: centre-loaded | distribution B: rim-loaded

teaching_path.action: Track the fall in gravitational energy into two destinations: centre motion and rotation about the centre.
teaching_path.why_valid: Pure rolling has both translational and rotational kinetic energy, so a larger rotational share leaves a smaller share for centre-of-mass motion at the same height loss.
teaching_path.output: same energy drop -> translation share + rotation share; rim-loaded case -> larger rotation share -> smaller centre-motion share

teaching_path.action: Repeat the comparison with the same shape at two different total masses while preserving the mass distribution relative to size.
teaching_path.why_valid: If the distribution pattern is unchanged, changing total mass alone does not create the shape-dependent ordering being tested in the ideal model.
teaching_path.output: same shape pattern + different total mass -> same ideal acceleration ordering

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The heavier rolling object reaches the bottom first because gravity pulls harder on it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two same-shape cylinders of different masses roll without slipping down the same incline. Which reaches the bottom first in the ideal model?
misconceptions.repair: Mass cancels from the ideal rolling-acceleration expression; the controlling shape information is I/(MR^2).

exit_task.prompt: Two equal-mass, equal-radius bodies roll without slipping from the same height. One is more rim-loaded. Predict which gains centre-of-mass speed more quickly and explain the role of mass distribution without calculating an acceleration.

answer.summary: The more centre-loaded body gains centre-of-mass speed more quickly because less of the common energy drop is tied up in rotation for the same translational progress.
reasoning: Both bodies begin with the same gravitational-energy change available over a given height loss.
Pure rolling requires energy to appear in both centre motion and rotation.
A distribution with greater rotational inertia demands a larger rotational share, leaving less for centre-of-mass motion.
answer.check: Compare two copies of the same shape at different masses; the ideal ordering should not reverse merely because one copy is heavier.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The response gives a qualitative acceleration ordering and energy-partition explanation without computing a numerical acceleration.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created qualitative rolling-energy comparison. The record deliberately avoids authoring the blocked acceleration equation or any gate-owned quantitative relation.

predict.prompt: Two bodies have the same mass and radius and start together down one incline without slipping. One keeps more mass near the rim. Must they arrive together?
predict.defensible_answer: No. In the ideal model the rim-loaded body devotes more of the energy change to rotation, so its centre speeds up less quickly.

attempt.produces: An energy-allocation diagram for two same-mass bodies showing a common input split differently between centre motion and rotation.

rubric.criterion: The energy input is held common before the split is compared.
rubric.evidence_of: The response isolates partition rather than changing the starting conditions.

rubric.criterion: The rim-loaded case assigns a larger share to rotation.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner connects distribution to rotational demand without blaming total mass.

accepted: Both cases start from the same height and show the same total energy drop; the rim-loaded case allocates more to rotation and less to centre motion.
rejected: The heavier-looking or visually larger object is declared faster without controlling mass, radius, and starting height, so no distribution effect has been isolated.

route.ask: What conditions must match before shape can be the reason one body accelerates differently?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents total mass or release height from becoming an uncontrolled explanation.

route.ask: Into what two motion forms can the common gravitational-energy decrease appear during pure rolling?
route.why_this_ask: It creates the partition the later comparison needs.

route.ask: Which distribution demands more rotational participation for the same overall motion?
route.why_this_ask: The learner connects radial distribution to the rotation share.

route.ask: What should happen if only total mass changes while shape stays similar?
route.why_this_ask: This boundary removes the tempting 'heavier is faster' explanation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path presents the two energy shares then checks mass scaling; the learner route first designs the fair comparison and only then decides how the common energy change is divided.

boundary_test.prompt: Two geometrically similar solid cylinders have different masses but roll ideally down the same incline from the same height. Should mass alone make one accelerate more?
boundary_test.answer: No. With the same shape pattern in the ideal no-slip model, changing total mass alone does not create a different acceleration.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner attributes the ideal acceleration difference to distribution relative to size, not to the magnitude of the gravitational force by itself.
