buckets.title: Current electricity: charge-flow foundation
buckets.badge_reason: Charge conservation must be separated from energy-transfer language before circuit equations are introduced.

capabilities.action: Track steady charge flow across the two boundaries of one unbranched circuit element.
capabilities.success_criterion: Explain why steady current entering and leaving the element must match when charge is not accumulating inside it.

capabilities.action: Test whether measured voltage-current pairs support one constant-resistance model under fixed conditions.
capabilities.success_criterion: From a small set of voltage-current pairs, decide whether the voltage-to-current ratio stays constant and state whether the constant-resistance model is supported.

microtopics.title: Charge flow is not consumed by a component
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday language about using electricity makes it easy to confuse energy transfer with disappearance of charge flow.
entry_assumptions: Can count charge carriers or total charge crossing a point over a time interval.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Current is a rate of charge passing a boundary; charge is not used up by a resistor.

teaching_path.action: Mark an entry boundary and an exit boundary around one component, and compare charge passage over matching time windows.
teaching_path.why_valid: Matching intervals make the two flow statements comparable; otherwise a difference could come only from observing for different lengths of time.
teaching_path.output: entry boundary = one count window; exit boundary = the same count window

teaching_path.action: Suppose the entry flow were persistently larger than the exit flow while the circuit stayed steady.
teaching_path.why_valid: The difference would have to remain inside the component as accumulating charge, so a permanent mismatch contradicts the stated steady condition.
teaching_path.output: more in than out -> charge pile-up; steady no-pile-up -> matching flow

teaching_path.action: Repeat the boundary comparison after replacing the component with a different ordinary component while keeping a single unbranched path.
teaching_path.why_valid: The conservation argument depends on the steady one-path condition, not on the component's particular construction.
teaching_path.output: single steady path -> same flow at entry and exit

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Current gets smaller after charge passes through a resistor.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: One ampere enters a resistor in a single unbranched path. In steady operation, what current leaves it?
misconceptions.repair: Track charge through the boundary: steady current cannot accumulate charge inside the resistor.

exit_task.prompt: A steady single-path circuit carries charge through one component. Say whether the charge-flow rate can be persistently smaller at the exit than at the entry and justify the answer without appealing to what the component does with energy.

answer.summary: It cannot be persistently smaller in the stated steady one-path case, because the missing charge would otherwise have to accumulate inside the component.
reasoning: Compare entry and exit over the same time window so the two flow statements refer to the same interval.
A sustained excess entering over leaving would increase the charge stored inside the component.
The stated steady condition excludes continuing accumulation, so the entry and exit flow rates must match.
answer.check: Ask where the difference would physically go if the two steady flow rates were unequal; if no accumulating store is allowed, the mismatch is inconsistent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer is a conservation argument about equality of steady flow, not a computation of a numerical electrical quantity.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created boundary ledger isolates charge conservation from later energy and circuit-law relations so the low rung can be reviewed independently.

predict.prompt: If a lamp glows in a steady one-path circuit, should less charge per second leave the lamp than entered it?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A lasting difference would imply charge continuously collecting inside the lamp.

attempt.produces: A boundary ledger showing what crosses into and out of one component during the same interval, plus a sentence accounting for any proposed mismatch.

rubric.criterion: The entry and exit observations use the same time interval.
rubric.evidence_of: Making the two flow-rate claims comparable.

rubric.criterion: Any proposed mismatch is traced to charge accumulation inside the component.
rubric.evidence_of: Using conservation rather than the vague claim that current stays the same.

accepted: The ledger compares matching windows and says a persistent excess entering would pile charge up inside, so a steady case requires matching entry and exit flow.
rejected: The response says the component uses some current and therefore less leaves, but names no place where the missing charge accumulates.

route.ask: What two boundaries would you watch if you wanted to know whether charge disappeared inside the component?
route.why_this_ask: It turns a vague flow idea into a closed accounting region.

route.ask: If more charge keeps entering than leaving, what must happen inside that region over time?
route.why_this_ask: The consequence of the misconception is easier to test than the rule itself.

route.ask: Does changing the component remove that accounting requirement while the path remains single and steady?
route.why_this_ask: It tests whether the learner attached the result to conservation rather than to one device.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path presents the boundary ledger; the elicitation route begins with the learner's own consumption prediction and makes them locate the supposedly missing charge.

boundary_test.prompt: Could entry and exit flow differ briefly while charge is building up on part of a circuit?
boundary_test.answer: Yes. The steady-state conclusion does not forbid a transient interval in which charge distribution is still changing.
boundary_test.confirms: The conservation claim is tied to the stated steady condition rather than asserted as an exceptionless slogan.

microtopics.title: Ohmic behavior is a tested model, not a permanent label
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must separate a measured proportional pattern from the stronger claim that every device keeps one resistance under every operating condition.
entry_assumptions: Can read paired voltage and current measurements for one device.
Can compare repeated ratios without treating a device name as evidence.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A constant-resistance Ohmic model is supported only when one device keeps the same voltage-to-current ratio across operating points while the relevant conditions are held fixed; changing the operating condition can make that model stop fitting.

teaching_path.action: Fix one device and one thermal condition, then place several measured voltage-current pairs in a table before naming any model.
teaching_path.why_valid: The model is a claim about a repeatable relationship under stated conditions, so device identity and condition must be held fixed before the measurements can test it.
teaching_path.output: same device + same thermal condition -> compare one V-I table

teaching_path.action: For the first table, divide each voltage by its paired current and compare the results.
teaching_path.why_valid: A single constant-resistance model predicts one unchanged proportionality across the measured operating points, so the repeated ratio is the direct test of that model.
teaching_path.output: 2/1 = 2 Ω; 4/2 = 2 Ω; 6/3 = 2 Ω -> one constant ratio

teaching_path.action: Repeat the same ratio check for a second table in which the device condition has changed, and refuse to carry the first model across automatically.
teaching_path.why_valid: Evidence collected under one condition does not authorize the same parameter under a changed condition; re-testing distinguishes a model from a permanent device label.
teaching_path.output: condition A: one ratio pattern; condition B: changed ratio pattern -> re-test the model

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every electrical component has one fixed resistance, so a constant-resistance model always applies.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If doubling the voltage more than doubles the current, is one constant ratio enough to describe the device over those measurements?
misconceptions.repair: Use the measured voltage-current pattern first; keep one constant resistance only when the ratio stays unchanged under the stated fixed conditions.

exit_task.prompt: Two voltage-current tables come from devices tested under fixed conditions. In table A the voltage-to-current ratio stays the same across all measured points; in table B it changes. Decide which table supports one constant-resistance Ohmic model and state the evidence.

answer.summary: Table A supports the constant-resistance model because its voltage-to-current ratio is unchanged across the measurements; table B does not because that ratio changes.
reasoning: Treat each table as evidence rather than assuming a model from the device name.
Compare the voltage-to-current ratio across every operating point in the same table.
Keep the constant-resistance model only for the table whose ratio remains unchanged under the stated fixed conditions.
answer.check: A different pair from the same table should lead to the same model decision; if one pair changes the ratio pattern, the constant-resistance claim is not supported over the full set.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer classifies whether a constant-ratio model is supported; it reports no computed resistance value.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created measurement-first construction isolates the model-validity distinction in the matrix without importing an ungated circuit equation as a library relation.

predict.prompt: A component is called a resistor. Before seeing any measurements, is that name enough to prove one constant resistance describes it at every operating point?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The constant-resistance claim must be tested against measured voltage-current pairs under stated conditions.

attempt.produces: A model decision for each of two V-I tables, with the repeated-ratio evidence written beside the decision.

rubric.criterion: The decision is based on whether the voltage-to-current ratio stays constant across all listed pairs.
rubric.evidence_of: Testing the model against the whole measured pattern rather than one convenient point.

rubric.criterion: The stated fixed condition is kept attached to the conclusion.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating constant resistance as a conditional model rather than a permanent device property.

accepted: Table A supports one constant resistance because the same ratio pattern persists at every measured point under the fixed condition; table B does not because its ratio pattern changes.
rejected: Both tables are called Ohmic because each contains voltage and current values; no comparison across operating points is made.

route.ask: What must stay fixed before measurements from different operating points can test one model?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents a condition change from being mistaken for failure or success of the same model.

route.ask: What comparison can you repeat for every voltage-current pair without assuming the answer first?
route.why_this_ask: The learner discovers the proportionality test from the data rather than receiving a device label.

route.ask: If that comparison is unchanged in one table and changes in another, which table supports one constant parameter?
route.why_this_ask: This turns the numerical pattern into the model-choice claim the rung teaches.

route.ask: What should you do after the device temperature changes?
route.why_this_ask: The final ask tests whether the learner understands the stated condition as part of the model.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path starts with a declared measurement condition and performs the ratio test; the elicitation route first challenges the device-label shortcut and makes the learner identify what evidence could justify the model.

boundary_test.prompt: If only one voltage-current pair has been measured, can that single point establish that the ratio will remain constant as the operating point changes?
boundary_test.answer: No. One point can be fitted by a constant parameter, but it cannot show that the same parameter persists across other operating points.
boundary_test.confirms: The rung is about evidence for a relationship across conditions, not about attaching a resistance label from one measurement.

entry_needs: Learners can count charge crossing a point during a stated interval.
learner_actions: Read a completed entry-and-exit boundary ledger.

help_plan: Keep the time windows matched.
Keep the accounting region visible around one component.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit the missing-charge contradiction
entry_needs: Learners can make a prediction about what enters and leaves a component.
learner_actions: Predict whether current is consumed.
Account for the missing charge if a mismatch is claimed.
Test the result against a transient boundary case.
Predict whether a device label alone justifies constant resistance, then reconstruct the repeated-ratio test from measurements.
help_plan: Ask where missing charge would go before revealing conservation.
Offer the boundary ledger only after the learner commits.
Close with the steady-versus-transient distinction.
Ask what evidence would distinguish a model from a permanent device label before showing the ratio comparison.

source_preferences.reason: The authored resource holds the prompts and model closure.

microtopics.title: A machine trades force or direction for distance; it does not create work
microtopics.badge_reason: A larger output force looks like an energy gain unless input distance is tracked.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish force from work and identify work as a force acting through displacement.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A simple machine can reduce effort force or change its direction by requiring a different input distance; in the ideal model input work equals useful output work.

teaching_path.action: Name the effort point, load point, effort force, load force, effort distance and load distance.
teaching_path.why_valid: Force advantage cannot be interpreted without identifying both input and output sides.
teaching_path.output: input: F_effort, d_effort; output: F_load, d_load.

teaching_path.action: For an ideal machine, compare the effort and load work using F_effort d_effort = F_load d_load.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-IDEAL-MACHINE-WORK owns the lossless input-output work equality.
teaching_path.output: F_effort d_effort = F_load d_load; if F_effort < F_load for the same ideal output work, then d_effort > d_load.

teaching_path.action: Double the load force advantage while keeping ideal useful output work fixed and ask what must happen to effort distance.
teaching_path.why_valid: The boundary exposes why force multiplication does not create energy.
teaching_path.output: greater force advantage -> compensating greater input distance in the ideal tradeoff.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a machine gives a larger output force than the effort force, it creates energy.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: An ideal machine doubles the output force. Can the effort point move the same distance as the load and still conserve work?
misconceptions.repair: Track both force and distance. In an ideal machine, a force advantage requires a compensating distance tradeoff.

exit_task.prompt: An ideal machine lets a person use a smaller effort force to raise a load. Without numbers, what must happen to the effort distance relative to the load distance if useful output work is unchanged?

answer.summary: The effort point must move farther than the load point when the effort force is smaller than the load force.
reasoning: Ideal input work equals useful output work.
Reducing input force while keeping output work fixed requires a larger input distance.
The machine trades force for distance rather than creating energy.
answer.check: If both force and distance were multiplied at the output with no extra input, output work would exceed input work and violate the ideal model.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit makes a qualitative ideal-work tradeoff claim without a computed value.

attempt.produces: An input/output force-distance comparison.

rubric.criterion: Tracks both force and distance.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating machine benefit as a tradeoff rather than free energy.

rubric.criterion: Keeps ideal input and useful output work equal.

accepted: Smaller effort force requires a longer effort distance for the same ideal output work.
rejected: The machine makes extra work because the load force is larger.

boundary_test.answer: No. Changing direction alone can be useful even without reducing the effort-force magnitude.

microtopics.title: Mechanical advantage is a same-state load-to-effort force ratio
microtopics.badge_reason: The ratio is simple; the fragile part is pairing load and effort from the same steady setup and not confusing force advantage with efficiency.
entry_assumptions: Can label input/effort and output/load forces on the same machine state.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Mechanical advantage is the dimensionless same-state force ratio MA = F_load/F_effort; a practical demonstration must measure both forces for one steady setup before forming the ratio, and the result says nothing by itself about efficiency.

teaching_path.action: Label the effort force and load force for one steady machine state before taking or using readings.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mechanical advantage compares simultaneous input/output force magnitudes for the same setup; mixing states makes the ratio physically meaningless.
teaching_path.output: one machine state with F_load and F_effort identified

teaching_path.action: Calculate MA = F_load/F_effort from those same-state force magnitudes.
teaching_path.why_valid: REL-MECHANICAL-ADVANTAGE owns the dimensionless load-to-effort ratio.
teaching_path.output: MA = F_load/F_effort

teaching_path.action: Check that the force units cancel and interpret MA = 1 and MA > 1 without making an efficiency claim.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both quantities are forces, so MA is dimensionless; its meaning is force advantage only.
teaching_path.output: MA dimensionless; MA = 1 means equal load/effort magnitudes; MA > 1 means force advantage

teaching_path.action: For a lever demonstration, measure load and effort for the same balanced or steady setting, then repeat under a controlled setup change while keeping the load and measurement method fixed.
teaching_path.why_valid: A fair practical comparison changes the intended machine setup while preventing mixed-state or mixed-method readings from masquerading as a mechanical-advantage change.
teaching_path.output: same-state MA measurement plus one controlled comparison

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Mechanical advantage is the same as efficiency.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can an ideal fixed pulley have MA = 1 and still be useful?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. MA compares forces only; a machine can be useful by changing force direction even with MA = 1.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A load reading from one lever setting can be divided by an effort reading from a different setting to calculate mechanical advantage.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the effort point is moved between two lever settings, may you combine the old load reading with the new effort reading to form one MA?
misconceptions.repair: No. Measure load and effort for the same steady setting, then calculate MA for that state. Compare separate same-state ratios across controlled settings.

exit_task.prompt: A machine lifts a 120 N load with a 40 N effort. Find the mechanical advantage and interpret it.

answer.summary: MA = 3. The load force is three times the effort force.
reasoning: MA = F_load/F_effort.
The ratio describes force advantage, not energy creation or efficiency.
answer.check: The newton units cancel, so MA is dimensionless.

boundary_test.answer: They are equal in magnitude; the machine provides no force multiplication.
boundary_test.confirms: Mechanical advantage is specifically a force ratio.

microtopics.title: Levers, pulleys and inclined planes realize different force-distance tradeoffs
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners can memorize device names without identifying what each machine changes about force, direction and distance.

microtopics.inferential_jump: A lever, pulley or inclined plane should be analysed by its input/output force, direction and distance tradeoff rather than by a memorized claim that every simple machine reduces force.

teaching_path.action: For each machine, identify the effort point/direction and the load motion.
teaching_path.why_valid: The same input-output language lets different machine types be compared without separate memorized rules.
teaching_path.output: lever, pulley and ramp each have named effort and load sides.

teaching_path.action: Compare whether the machine mainly changes force magnitude, force direction, or required input distance in the stated setup.
teaching_path.why_valid: Simple-machine benefit is a geometric/input-output tradeoff, not a universal force reduction.
teaching_path.output: fixed pulley may change direction; force-advantage setups require extra input distance; incline spreads a height gain over a longer path.

teaching_path.action: Use an ideal fixed pulley as the counterexample to 'all machines reduce effort force'.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction-changing machine can be useful with no force multiplication.
teaching_path.output: machine usefulness can be directional even when MA = 1.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Every pulley, lever or inclined plane must reduce the effort force.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What useful change can an ideal fixed pulley provide even when effort and load force magnitudes are equal?
misconceptions.repair: It can reverse the direction of the required effort. Identify the actual setup before claiming force advantage.

exit_task.prompt: Compare an ideal fixed pulley with a long inclined plane used to raise the same load. State one useful change each machine can provide without claiming that either creates energy.

answer.summary: The fixed pulley can change the effort direction; the inclined plane can reduce the required force by spreading the same height gain over a longer input path.
reasoning: The fixed pulley can redirect the pull even when force magnitude is not reduced.
The incline increases the distance over which the load reaches the same height.
Both are input-output tradeoffs consistent with work conservation in the ideal model.
answer.check: Neither description requires useful output work to exceed ideal input work.

microtopics.title: One magnetic direction, several page marks
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must coordinate a three-dimensional axial direction with two-dimensional page marks before later magnetic rules are readable.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish a location in a diagram from a direction assigned at that location.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Magnetic field B is an axial vector: its direction is tied to an oriented rotation convention, and dot/cross marks encode out-of-page and into-page directions rather than particle paths.

teaching_path.action: Fix the page convention before interpreting the drawing: a dot means toward the viewer and a cross means away from the viewer.
teaching_path.why_valid: The marks are projections of one directed quantity; declaring their viewing meaning first prevents a symbol from being mistaken for a physical object.
teaching_path.output: dot = toward viewer; cross = away from viewer

teaching_path.action: Turn the same physical setup so a direction that was drawn in the page now points toward the viewer, then redraw only its direction mark.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing the viewpoint changes the page mark while leaving the physical direction fixed, so agreement across the two drawings tests interpretation rather than memorization.
teaching_path.output: same physical B: in-page arrow -> dot after the viewpoint turns

teaching_path.action: Trace one direction line around and through a bar magnet instead of stopping at a pole.
teaching_path.why_valid: A direction map must remain continuous; following the same line through the material exposes the error in treating the outside segment as an endpoint.
teaching_path.output: outside N -> S; inside S -> N; no endpoint

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Magnetic field lines begin at a north pole and end at a south pole everywhere.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Trace one magnetic field line through and around a bar magnet. Where can it stop?
misconceptions.repair: Treat field lines as a direction map: they continue in closed loops, including through the magnet.

exit_task.prompt: A diagram shows one magnetic direction once as an arrow and once with a page mark after the view is changed. Explain how both can describe the same physical direction and say whether the associated direction line may terminate at a pole.

answer.summary: The page mark changes with the view, but the physical magnetic direction does not; a field-direction line is continued through the magnet rather than terminated at a pole.
reasoning: Bind every page mark to the declared viewing convention instead of reading dot or cross as an object.
Compare the physical direction before and after the viewpoint change; only its two-dimensional depiction has changed.
Continue the direction line through the magnet so the apparent outside endpoint is seen as part of a closed path.
answer.check: Rotate the imagined viewpoint back. The mark should recover the original arrow direction, and tracing the same line should never require an endpoint.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer makes a directional classification and continuity argument; it asserts no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created bridge from page notation to axial direction needs subject and pedagogical review before promotion.

predict.prompt: If an arrow that points toward you is redrawn after the page is turned, must the physical magnetic direction have changed?
predict.defensible_answer: No. The page symbol can change because the view changed while the physical direction in space stays fixed.

attempt.produces: A pair of sketches of the same magnetic direction from two viewpoints, plus one continuously traced line around and through a bar magnet.

rubric.criterion: The two sketches use the declared dot/cross meanings consistently.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping physical direction separate from the mark used to display it.

rubric.criterion: The traced line continues through the magnet rather than ending at a pole.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing a field-line drawing as a continuous direction map.

rejected: A dot is labelled as a particle coming out of the magnet and the traced line is stopped at the south pole, so representation marks are treated as physical endpoints.

boundary_test.confirms: The page convention represents a three-dimensional direction rather than decorating a two-dimensional sketch.

microtopics.title: Through-going field depends on surface orientation
microtopics.badge_reason: The hard move is treating the surface as oriented and comparing how much field passes through it without changing either its size or the field.
entry_assumptions: R1: magnetic field B is an axial directed quantity with explicit in-plane and out-of-plane representation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Magnetic flux measures the component of magnetic field through an oriented area; changing the surface orientation changes flux even when B and area size stay fixed.

teaching_path.action: Attach a normal arrow to the surface before comparing orientations, so the face has an explicit through-direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: A flat surface alone has no preferred side; the normal supplies the orientation needed to distinguish with-through from against-through.
teaching_path.output: surface orientation = chosen normal direction

teaching_path.action: Rotate the same loop from face-on to tilted to edge-on while leaving its size and the surrounding field unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only orientation changes, so any change in through-going field is attributable to how the surface faces the field rather than to a stronger field or larger loop.
teaching_path.output: face-on -> most through; tilted -> less through; edge-on -> none through

teaching_path.action: Keep the physical surface fixed but reverse which normal arrow is declared positive.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing the chosen orientation reverses the sign convention while leaving the physical setup unchanged, separating signed description from apparatus.
teaching_path.output: normal one way -> one sign; reversed normal -> opposite sign

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Flux is just magnetic-field strength times area, so orientation does not matter.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A loop with fixed area rotates from face-on to edge-on in a uniform field. What must happen to its flux?
misconceptions.repair: Project the oriented area along the field direction: the dot product selects the component through the surface.

exit_task.prompt: Three identical loops sit in the same uniform magnetic field: one face-on, one tilted, and one edge-on. Rank the amount of field passing through them and explain the role of the chosen surface normal.

answer.summary: The face-on loop has the greatest through-going field, the tilted loop has less, and the edge-on loop has none; the normal states which side counts as the positive orientation.
reasoning: The field strength and loop area are held fixed, so orientation is the only changing feature.
A face presented to the field admits the greatest through-going component, while an edge presented to it admits none.
Reversing the named normal changes the sign convention but not the physical loop or field.
answer.check: Imagine rotating only the loop continuously from face-on to edge-on; the ranking should change smoothly without any appeal to a stronger or weaker field.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer ranks orientations and explains sign choice qualitatively; it contains no computed numerical result.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created orientation sequence makes the matrix's flux distinction teachable without asserting an ungated flux equation.

predict.prompt: If the field and loop size stay fixed, can simply turning the loop change how much field passes through its face?
predict.defensible_answer: Yes. Turning the loop changes how its oriented face meets the field even though neither magnitude nor area changes.

attempt.produces: Three sketches of the same loop at face-on, tilted, and edge-on orientations, each with a normal arrow and a qualitative through-going ranking.

rubric.criterion: Only orientation changes across the three sketches.
rubric.evidence_of: Isolating orientation as the cause of the changed through-going field.

rubric.criterion: Every sketch carries an explicit normal arrow.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating the surface as oriented rather than as an unsigned patch.

accepted: The same-sized loop is shown in all three cases, with face-on ranked above tilted and edge-on ranked at none, and every face has a declared normal.
rejected: The face-on case is drawn with a larger loop or stronger field, so the ranking can no longer be attributed to orientation alone.

route.ask: What arrow could you attach to the face so 'through this side' has a definite meaning?
route.why_this_ask: This elicits the need for an oriented surface before naming it.

route.ask: If you reverse only that arrow, what changed physically and what changed only in the description?
route.why_this_ask: It separates sign convention from the unchanged apparatus.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path supplies a normal first; the elicitation route starts from an unexplained orientation effect and makes the learner invent the missing face-direction needed to describe it.

boundary_test.prompt: What happens to the through-going field when the loop is exactly edge-on to the field?
boundary_test.answer: It reaches the limiting case of none passing through the face even though the field itself remains present and unchanged.
boundary_test.confirms: The comparison depends on how the surface faces the field, not merely on field presence.

microtopics.title: A perpendicular magnetic force redirects without speeding up
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often transfer the everyday rule 'force means speeding up' to a case where force is everywhere sideways to the instantaneous motion.
entry_assumptions: Can distinguish a velocity arrow's direction from its length.
Can recognize perpendicular directions and interpret a zero dot product geometrically.
microtopics.inferential_jump: When the magnetic force is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, it can continually turn the velocity arrow without lengthening or shortening it; the magnetic interaction redirects motion without supplying kinetic energy.

teaching_path.action: At one instant, draw the velocity arrow tangent to the path and the magnetic-force arrow perpendicular to it.
teaching_path.why_valid: The rung's claim applies to a pure magnetic interaction in the stated perpendicular case, so the local force-versus-velocity geometry must be fixed before any conclusion about speed is made.
teaching_path.output: instant 1: v -> ; F ⟂ v

teaching_path.action: Advance a short time step and redraw the velocity with a changed direction but the same arrow length, while keeping the force sideways to the new velocity.
teaching_path.why_valid: A sideways change alters direction while preserving the magnitude represented by arrow length; repeating that local update builds a curved path without a speed increase.
teaching_path.output: |v₁| = |v₂| ; direction(v₁) ≠ direction(v₂)

teaching_path.action: Use the dot-product check on the force and instantaneous velocity at each snapshot.
teaching_path.why_valid: Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product, so the magnetic force has no component along the motion to supply or remove kinetic energy.
teaching_path.output: F ⟂ v -> F·v = 0 -> magnetic contribution to speed change = 0

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A magnetic field makes a charged particle speed up simply because a force acts on it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A particle curves in a uniform pure magnetic field. If its speed rises, what interaction supplied the extra kinetic energy?
misconceptions.repair: Compare the force with the instantaneous velocity: a perpendicular magnetic force turns the motion, while its zero dot product with velocity means it does not add kinetic energy.

exit_task.prompt: A particle moves through a region where the only force is magnetic and is perpendicular to its instantaneous velocity. State what may change about the velocity and what must remain unchanged, and justify the answer with the force-velocity geometry.

answer.summary: The velocity direction may change, so the path can curve, but the speed and kinetic energy remain unchanged because the magnetic force has no component along the instantaneous motion.
reasoning: Read speed from the length of the velocity arrow and direction from where that arrow points.
A force perpendicular to the velocity changes the direction of the arrow rather than its length in the ideal pure-magnetic case.
The perpendicular force-velocity dot product is zero, which is the work-or-power check that no kinetic energy is transferred by the magnetic force.
answer.check: Compare two nearby snapshots: the tangent direction should rotate while the velocity-arrow length stays fixed and the force remains perpendicular to the local tangent.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer distinguishes direction, speed, and kinetic-energy changes qualitatively; it computes no magnetic-force magnitude or trajectory radius.

microtopics.research_contribution: This author-created local-snapshot construction teaches the work-free redirection distinction without importing a quantitative Lorentz-force magnitude or circular-motion relation.

predict.prompt: A force is acting on a moving charge, but the force arrow is exactly sideways to the velocity arrow. Must the particle be getting faster?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A sideways force can change the direction of motion while leaving the speed unchanged.

attempt.produces: Two successive velocity-force snapshots on a curved path, with the velocity-arrow lengths compared and a force-velocity dot-product check.

rubric.criterion: The later velocity arrow changes direction without changing length.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating redirection from speeding up.

rubric.criterion: The force is kept perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity and the dot-product check is identified as zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Connecting the geometry to the no-energy-transfer conclusion.

accepted: The path bends, the two velocity arrows have equal lengths, each force arrow is sideways to the local velocity, and the response uses the zero dot product to explain unchanged kinetic energy.
rejected: The later velocity arrow is longer solely because a force exists, even though the force is drawn perpendicular to the motion.

route.ask: Which feature of a velocity arrow represents speed, and which represents direction?

route.ask: If the force is exactly sideways, what could change about the velocity arrow without changing its length?
route.why_this_ask: This makes redirection the learner's construction rather than a stated rule.

route.why_this_ask: The geometric check closes the work-or-power claim without asking for a force magnitude.

route.ask: If the field strength changed while the force stayed perpendicular, which conclusion survives?
route.why_this_ask: It tests the invariant distinction: curvature may change, but the pure magnetic interaction still does not supply kinetic energy.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path starts from a declared perpendicular snapshot; the elicitation route first asks the learner to separate velocity length from direction, then makes the curved-path construction emerge from that distinction.

boundary_test.prompt: If an additional non-magnetic force has a component along the velocity, may the speed still be assumed constant?
boundary_test.answer: No. The no-speed-change conclusion belongs to the pure magnetic perpendicular-force case; an additional along-motion force can transfer kinetic energy.
boundary_test.confirms: The rung's conclusion is conditional on the stated force geometry and does not claim that every curved charged-particle path has constant speed.

microtopics.title: Impose a component constraint on a resultant
microtopics.badge_reason: The learner must reverse the usual direction of reasoning: instead of finding the resultant from inputs, one resultant component is specified and an input component must be chosen to make it true.
entry_assumptions: Can add vectors component by component in a common axis system.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A requested resultant direction can be translated into a component condition, such as zero along one axis, and that condition can be solved before any magnitude or travel-time calculation.

teaching_path.action: Translate the requested resultant direction into a component condition on the declared axes.
teaching_path.why_valid: A resultant exactly perpendicular to one axis has zero component along that axis.
teaching_path.output: For a direct-across resultant, the along-stream resultant component is set to zero.

teaching_path.action: Write the component-sum equation for that axis using all contributing vectors with their signs.
teaching_path.why_valid: The resultant component equals the sum of the input components on the same axis.
teaching_path.output: R_x=A_x+B_x, with the stated target substituted for R_x.

teaching_path.action: Solve the signed input component required to satisfy the target.
teaching_path.why_valid: The constraint equation determines the compensating component directly.
teaching_path.output: If R_x=0, then the required compensating input is A_x=-B_x.

teaching_path.action: Substitute the solved component back into the sum and confirm the constrained resultant component.
teaching_path.why_valid: Direct substitution checks both sign and axis choice without relying on the story wording.
teaching_path.output: The constrained component evaluates to the requested target.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: To make a resultant point directly across, each contributing vector must itself point directly across.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can one vector have an along-stream component if another vector has an equal opposite along-stream component?
misconceptions.repair: Apply the condition to the resultant, not each input. Opposite signed components can cancel while the individual vectors remain angled.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A zero resultant component means all motion or all vector magnitude is zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the resultant x-component is zero but the y-component is positive, is the resultant the zero vector?
misconceptions.repair: A component constraint applies to one axis only. The resultant can still be nonzero on the perpendicular axis.

exit_task.prompt: In one frame, a current contributes +3 along the x-axis. Choose the swimmer's x-component so the combined velocity has x-component 0, and state the equation you used.

answer.summary: The swimmer must contribute -3 along x, because 0=(-3)+3.
reasoning: The target is a zero x-component for the resultant.
The resultant x-component is the signed sum of swimmer and current x-components.
Setting 0=v_swimmer,x+3 gives v_swimmer,x=-3.
answer.check: Substitute -3 back into the x-component sum and verify it equals zero.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is a signed one-axis constraint check; any later magnitude or angle calculation is deliberately outside this capability.

microtopics.research_contribution: This constraint formulation is author-created to isolate a reusable vector-composition move exposed by real river-crossing demand; it does not promote the external question bank to curriculum authority.

predict.prompt: A current contributes +3 along x. If the resultant must have no x-component, should the swimmer's x-component have the same sign or the opposite sign?
predict.defensible_answer: Opposite sign, so the two x-components can cancel.

attempt.produces: A one-axis component equation with the target resultant value and the solved compensating input component.

rubric.criterion: Writes the resultant component as a signed sum of the input components.
rubric.evidence_of: Applying vector composition to the constrained axis.

rubric.criterion: Solves the compensating component with the opposite sign.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the target condition rather than forcing each input to zero.

rejected: v_x=0 because the boat must go directly across; this incorrectly applies the resultant condition to one input vector.

route.why_this_ask: It turns the verbal direction into an axis condition.

boundary_test.answer: Zero.
boundary_test.confirms: The compensating component exists only to satisfy the resultant constraint; it is not an intrinsic river-crossing rule.

microtopics.title: Add vectors by corresponding signed components
microtopics.badge_reason: The arithmetic is simple once the representation is correct, but learners often add magnitudes or mix unlike axes instead of combining corresponding signed components.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed vector components against declared axes.
Can distinguish a vector from its magnitude.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Vector addition preserves direction information by combining each axis independently; magnitude-only addition is only valid in special collinear cases.

teaching_path.action: Put both vectors in the same declared x-y axis system and write each as a signed component pair.
teaching_path.why_valid: Corresponding components can only be combined when they refer to the same axes and positive directions.
teaching_path.output: A=(A_x,A_y), B=(B_x,B_y) in one common axis system.

teaching_path.action: Add corresponding signed components: x with x and y with y.
teaching_path.why_valid: Vector addition is component-wise in a common basis, so each axis contribution combines independently.
teaching_path.output: A+B=(A_x+B_x, A_y+B_y).

teaching_path.action: Check the resultant direction from the component signs and compare with the rough tail-to-head geometry.
teaching_path.why_valid: The component pair and graphical resultant are two representations of the same vector and must agree in orientation.
teaching_path.output: A signed resultant pair whose quadrant/direction agrees with the arrow construction.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The magnitude of A+B is always |A|+|B|.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two equal vectors point in opposite directions. Must their resultant magnitude equal the sum of their two magnitudes?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the directions by using signed components or a tail-to-head diagram. Opposite components cancel instead of adding as positive sizes.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any two component numbers can be added if they come from the two vectors.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Should an x-component from A ever be added directly to a y-component from B when the axes are unchanged?
misconceptions.repair: Match axis with axis: x contributions combine only with x contributions, and y only with y.

exit_task.prompt: In one east-positive, north-positive frame, A=(3,4) and B=(-5,2). State A+B as signed components and describe the resultant's horizontal and vertical directions.

answer.summary: A+B=(-2,6): the resultant points westward and northward in the declared frame.
reasoning: Add horizontal components: 3+(-5)=-2.
Add vertical components: 4+2=6.
Negative x means west and positive y means north under the declared axes.
answer.check: A rough tail-to-head sketch should end left of and above the start.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: All component values are declared in the prompt; the task checks component-wise composition and sign interpretation.

microtopics.research_contribution: The component-wise vector-addition rule is standard; this numerical teaching sequence is author-created and remains pending independent scientific/pedagogical review.

predict.prompt: A points mostly northeast and B has a larger westward than eastward horizontal contribution. Before calculating, which horizontal sign do you expect for A+B?
predict.defensible_answer: Negative/westward, because the westward horizontal contribution is larger in magnitude.

attempt.produces: One signed resultant component pair plus a short axis-by-axis addition.

rubric.criterion: Adds only corresponding components.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating vector addition as axis-wise composition.

rubric.criterion: Preserves negative signs through the arithmetic.
rubric.evidence_of: Retaining directional information rather than adding magnitudes.

rejected: (8,6), which turns the westward component into a positive size before adding.

route.ask: Which numbers describe horizontal contributions in the common frame?
route.why_this_ask: It restores axis matching before any arithmetic.

route.ask: What is the signed horizontal total? What is the signed vertical total?
route.why_this_ask: It rebuilds the vector one axis at a time.

route.ask: Do those two signs agree with where a tail-to-head sketch should end?

boundary_test.answer: The zero vector: every component cancels.
boundary_test.confirms: Corresponding signed components, not magnitudes, are what combine in vector addition.

microtopics.title: Operand order reverses a subtraction result
microtopics.badge_reason: The construction may already be familiar, but learners can still preserve the same arrow direction after swapping the words.
entry_assumptions: Can construct one graphical subtraction by reversing the second arrow before tail-to-head addition.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Swapping which directed quantity comes first in a subtraction reverses the result's direction while leaving its length unchanged.

teaching_path.action: Write two ordered requests for the same pair: A minus B, then B minus A.
teaching_path.why_valid: Keeping the pair fixed isolates order as the only change.
teaching_path.output: case 1: A minus B.  case 2: B minus A.

teaching_path.action: For A minus B, follow A and then the reversed B arrow using the already-learned subtraction construction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The prerequisite construction gives a directed result for the stated order without introducing a new rule.
teaching_path.output: A - B -> one completed arrow from the common start to the construction endpoint.

teaching_path.action: Repeat with the order swapped and place both completed arrows from the same start for comparison.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only the order changed, so direct superposition exposes what order does to orientation.
teaching_path.output: B minus A: same drawn length as the first result, pointing exactly the opposite way.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Vector subtraction is commutative in the same way as vector addition.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If A minus B points east, must B minus A point east too?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the same two inputs, swap only their order, and compare the two completed arrows from one start; the second points opposite the first.

exit_task.prompt: Two labelled arrows A and B are shown, and a completed construction for A minus B points southeast. Without recalculating its length, describe the direction of B minus A and explain the check you used.

answer.summary: B minus A points northwest: exactly opposite to the shown result, with the same length.
reasoning: The two requests use the same pair and differ only in order.
Swapping the order swaps which arrow is reversed in the known construction.
Placing both results from one start makes the second point opposite the first.
answer.check: Swap the labels again; the direction must return to southeast without changing the length.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer asserts no computed magnitude. It checks the qualitative reversal caused by swapping operand order.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created distinction layered on the existing graphical-subtraction capability. The candidate packet was consulted as non-authoritative input; no packet claim is promoted.

predict.prompt: A minus B has already been drawn pointing southeast. Before drawing anything else, where do you expect B minus A to point?
predict.defensible_answer: Northwest, because swapping the order reverses the completed directed result while keeping its length.

attempt.produces: A second arrow, drawn from the same start as the first, showing the predicted direction for B minus A plus one sentence naming what changed.

rubric.criterion: The second arrow points exactly opposite the first.
rubric.evidence_of: Treating operand order as directional information.

rubric.criterion: The explanation says order changed while the input pair stayed fixed.
rubric.evidence_of: Isolating the cause of the reversal instead of appealing to a memorized sign change.

accepted: A northwest arrow from the same start, the same length as the southeast arrow, with the note 'same pair; order swapped, so direction reverses.'
rejected: Another southeast arrow labelled B minus A. This treats subtraction as if swapping operands left the directed result unchanged.

route.ask: Which of the two original arrows is second in A minus B, and what does the construction do to that second arrow?
route.why_this_ask: It reconnects the new order question to the already-owned graphical construction.

route.ask: Now make B the first quantity. Which arrow is second this time?
route.why_this_ask: The learner has to identify the single structural change before seeing the result.

route.ask: Draw the swapped-order result from the same start as the first. Which way does it point relative to the first?
route.why_this_ask: Superposition turns the order change into a visible orientation change.

route.ask: What stayed unchanged when the order swapped?
route.why_this_ask: Naming the unchanged length prevents the learner from treating reversal as an unrelated second calculation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path demonstrates both orders. The learner route begins with a prediction from one completed order, then reconstructs the second and uses superposition to test the prediction.

boundary_test.prompt: Suppose A and B are identical arrows. What do both subtraction orders produce, and what happens to the idea of an opposite direction?
boundary_test.answer: Both give the zero result. Its length is zero, so there is no direction to reverse.
boundary_test.confirms: The reversal statement applies to a directed nonzero result; the zero case is the limiting boundary.

microtopics.title: Resolve magnitude-and-angle vectors into signed perpendicular components
microtopics.badge_reason: The trigonometry is short, but learners must first decide whether decomposition is needed, identify the angle reference, preserve signs, and avoid treating an initial component pair as a later-time motion law.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed components against declared axes.
Basic sine/cosine right-triangle ratios are available through the declared Mathematics bridge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: A magnitude-and-angle description and a signed perpendicular-component pair can represent the same vector. Projection converts between those representations; it does not by itself describe how a vector such as velocity changes later in time.

teaching_path.action: Decide whether the vector still needs decomposition. If it is given by magnitude plus angle, declare the perpendicular axes and mark exactly which axis the angle is measured from; if signed components are already supplied, keep them rather than applying trigonometry again.
teaching_path.why_valid: Projection is a representation conversion, not a compulsory formula step. The angle reference and axis convention determine which projection geometry is relevant.
teaching_path.output: representation decision + declared axes + explicit angle reference

teaching_path.action: Identify which component direction is adjacent to the stated angle and which is opposite before writing sine or cosine.
teaching_path.why_valid: Cosine and sine attach to adjacent/opposite geometry; x and y receive those labels only after the reference axis is known.
teaching_path.output: adjacent component identified; opposite component identified

teaching_path.action: Compute the component magnitudes with V cos(theta) for the adjacent leg and V sin(theta) for the opposite leg.
teaching_path.why_valid: The original vector magnitude is the right-triangle hypotenuse and the perpendicular component magnitudes are its projections.
teaching_path.output: V_adj = V cos(theta); V_opp = V sin(theta)

teaching_path.action: Attach signs from the declared positive directions and label the pair with the vector role named by the problem; for an initial velocity this means u_x and u_y at the chosen initial instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Projection gives component magnitudes, while the coordinate frame supplies signs and the problem context supplies the state label. The decomposition itself does not license any later-time evolution claim.
teaching_path.output: signed, role-bound component pair such as (V_x,V_y) or initial (u_x,u_y)

teaching_path.action: Reconstruct the original magnitude and check that the component signs/quadrant agree with the drawn vector.
teaching_path.why_valid: A correct decomposition is an equivalent representation of the same vector, so magnitude and orientation must be consistent.
teaching_path.output: component pair independently checked against original vector

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The x-component is always V cos(theta), regardless of which axis theta is measured from.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If theta is measured from the +y axis instead of +x, which component is adjacent to theta?
misconceptions.repair: Name the angle reference first. Cosine goes with the adjacent component and sine with the opposite component; x/y labels follow only after the geometry is fixed.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Sine and cosine automatically provide the component signs.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A vector points left and upward. If its acute reference angle is used in a right triangle, must both resolved components be positive?
misconceptions.repair: Use trigonometry for component magnitudes, then use the declared axis directions to attach signs.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Whenever a vector question contains components, trigonometric decomposition must be performed.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A velocity is already supplied as (-6 i + 8 j) m/s. Is another sine/cosine decomposition required before using those components?
misconceptions.repair: No. The vector is already in component form. Decomposition is needed when converting from a magnitude-angle description to components.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: After an initial velocity is resolved into u_x and u_y, vector decomposition proves that both components keep those same values later.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Does writing u_y=u sin(theta) at launch prove that v_y remains u_y during later projectile motion?
misconceptions.repair: No. Decomposition describes the initial vector only. Later velocity components are determined by the motion model; vector decomposition does not supply that evolution.

exit_task.prompt: A launch velocity of magnitude 20 m/s points 30 degrees above +x. Resolve only the initial velocity into signed components, label them correctly, and state what this calculation does not yet tell you about later motion.

answer.summary: u_x=20 cos(30°)=10√3 m/s and u_y=20 sin(30°)=10 m/s, both positive. These are the t=0 velocity components; decomposition alone does not determine their later values.
reasoning: The angle is measured from +x, so x is adjacent and y is opposite.
The vector points right and up, so both initial component signs are positive.
Label the pair u_x,u_y because the problem names an initial velocity.
Any later v_x,v_y requires a motion model in addition to this representation step.
answer.check: sqrt(u_x^2+u_y^2)=20 m/s and the signs place the vector in the first quadrant.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exact components follow directly from the declared 20 m/s, 30° vector; the final sentence is a scope boundary, not a claim about a particular projectile model.

microtopics.research_contribution: Selected Motion-in-a-Plane demand makes magnitude-angle decomposition a genuine upstream prerequisite. Common PR #350 also separates the projectile REPRESENT step from later model evolution. This packet keeps that boundary: Vectors owns representation conversion; Motion-in-2D owns time evolution.

predict.prompt: Before calculating, if an acute angle is measured from +y, which component should use cosine: x or y?
predict.defensible_answer: The y-component magnitude, because y is adjacent to the stated angle.

attempt.produces: A representation decision, labelled vector sketch, and signed component pair with the correct contextual labels.

rubric.criterion: Checks whether decomposition is needed before applying trigonometry.
rubric.evidence_of: Distinguishing representation choice from mechanical formula use.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the angle reference and adjacent/opposite components before sine/cosine.
rubric.evidence_of: Correct projection geometry.

rubric.criterion: Applies signs from the declared axes and uses the problem's vector-role labels.
rubric.evidence_of: Preserving direction and state meaning.

accepted: From +x in quadrant I: V_x=V cos(theta), V_y=V sin(theta); for launch velocity label these u_x,u_y at t=0.
rejected: Always write x=V cos(theta) without checking the angle reference, or assume resolved initial components are automatically later-time constants.

microtopics.title: Split one plane-motion event into independent x/y components with one clock
microtopics.badge_reason: Learners often interpret independent components as unrelated motions and accidentally use different times or mix x and y quantities.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed vector components in a declared x-y frame.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Perpendicular components may be solved separately because each axis equation contains only that axis's quantities, but they still describe one object at one physical time.

teaching_path.action: Choose one fixed x-y frame, one origin and one time origin for the whole plane-motion event.
teaching_path.why_valid: A component value is meaningful only after its frame and sign convention are fixed.
teaching_path.output: one declared frame, origin, axis orientation and t=0

teaching_path.action: Represent position, velocity and acceleration as signed x and y components in that same frame.
teaching_path.why_valid: A plane vector is completely represented by its perpendicular Cartesian components once the frame is declared.
teaching_path.output: signed component state (x,y), (v_x,v_y), (a_x,a_y)

teaching_path.action: Keep x-quantities in the x description and y-quantities in the y description while using one shared elapsed time.
teaching_path.why_valid: The perpendicular component equations are independent in Cartesian kinematics, but both describe the same object during the same physical interval.
teaching_path.output: two axis histories coupled by one clock

teaching_path.action: Recombine only component values that refer to the same frame and the same instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mixing x at one time with y at another does not describe any single physical state of the object.
teaching_path.output: one physically valid plane state reconstructed from simultaneous components

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Independent x and y motions may use different elapsed times.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At one instant 2 s after launch, may the x equation use t=2 s while the y equation uses another time?
misconceptions.repair: No. Independence separates the axis equations; it does not give the same object two clocks.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The x-motion and y-motion are two different objects that can be paired arbitrarily later.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: May x(2 s) be combined with y(3 s) to describe the particle's position?
misconceptions.repair: No. A plane state is a simultaneous pair. Recombine x(t) and y(t) only at the same t in the same frame.

reasoning: Keep x quantities in the x equation and y quantities in the y equation.
Use one common elapsed time for the same physical instant.
Recombine components only after each axis is handled consistently.
answer.check: Both component values must refer to the same frame and same instant.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If one acceleration component is constant, the constant-acceleration equations are automatically valid on both axes.

reasoning: Read signed component initial velocities and accelerations.
Apply the 1D constant-acceleration displacement relation separately.
Keep one common elapsed time.
answer.check: Units are metres on both displacements and no x quantity appears in the y equation or vice versa.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The task asks for exact symbolic setup, not a new numerical claim.

microtopics.research_contribution: Directly matches ExamSIDE 2020 x-y constant-acceleration demand while reusing the existing 1D constant-acceleration capability rather than duplicating it.

predict.prompt: If a_x is nonzero and a_y is zero, which velocity component changes with time?
predict.defensible_answer: Only v_x changes; v_y remains constant.

attempt.produces: Two correct component constant-acceleration equations using one t.

rubric.criterion: Each axis uses only its own signed initial values and acceleration while sharing the same time.
rubric.evidence_of: 2D component model use rather than a scalar-magnitude shortcut.

accepted: v_x=u_x+a_x t and v_y=u_y+a_y t with one t.
rejected: Use |a| in both equations or use separate unrelated times.

route.ask: Before using a constant-acceleration formula, what must be true about that axis's acceleration component?
route.why_this_ask: Makes model validity explicit rather than formula-driven.

boundary_test.prompt: If a_y changes with time while a_x stays constant, may the constant-acceleration equations still be exact on both axes for the whole interval?
boundary_test.answer: No. The x relation may remain exact, but the y constant-acceleration relation is not exact over that interval.
boundary_test.confirms: Model validity is checked per component.

microtopics.title: Select the gravity-only projectile model before using projectile consequences
microtopics.badge_reason: Projectile formulas become brittle when the learner skips the model decision, mixes times, or treats horizontal velocity as requiring a continuing horizontal force.
entry_assumptions: Can solve 2D constant-acceleration component equations.
If an oblique launch angle is given, angle-based vector decomposition is available as a separate prerequisite for that question.
microtopics.inferential_jump: After release in the ideal near-Earth model, projectile motion is not a new set of laws: it is the same component kinematics with a_x=0 and a_y=-g (for +y upward).

teaching_path.action: Decide whether the object is in ideal near-Earth free flight after release; neglect air resistance, declare +y, then set a_x=0 and a_y=-g.
teaching_path.why_valid: The standard projectile equations are a conditional specialization of 2D constant acceleration, not an automatic label for every launched object.
teaching_path.output: gravity-only projectile acceleration state

teaching_path.action: Use supplied or separately resolved u_x and u_y with one common t in the horizontal and vertical component equations.
teaching_path.why_valid: Horizontal, oblique and downward/upward initial components change the initial state, not the gravity-only model.
teaching_path.output: v_x=u_x; v_y=u_y-g t; Delta x=u_x t; Delta y=u_y t-0.5g t^2

teaching_path.action: Translate the requested event into the component condition that defines it before solving for time.
teaching_path.why_valid: Apex, same-height return, ground impact and a specified later instant are different events; each is identified by a different component condition.
teaching_path.output: event condition chosen before calculation

teaching_path.action: For an apex event, set v_y=0 while keeping v_x=u_x and a_y=-g.
teaching_path.why_valid: At the highest point only the vertical velocity component is momentarily zero; gravity still accelerates downward and horizontal motion continues.
teaching_path.output: apex condition v_y=0 with nonzero horizontal velocity and nonzero downward acceleration

teaching_path.action: For a return to the launch height, set Delta y=0 and treat any same-height flight-time/range shortcut as conditional on that equality.
teaching_path.why_valid: The shortcut follows from the vertical displacement returning to its initial value; it is not valid when the landing height differs.
teaching_path.output: same-height event condition and its validity boundary

teaching_path.action: For a horizontal launch or unequal-height landing, use u_y=0 only as the initial vertical condition and obtain the event time from the vertical position equation.
teaching_path.why_valid: Gravity immediately builds vertical velocity; the fall/landing condition, not the horizontal speed, determines the flight time.
teaching_path.output: vertical event time for horizontal or unequal-height launch

teaching_path.action: At the selected event time, reconstruct the requested velocity, speed, direction, displacement or range from simultaneous components and check qualitative limits.
teaching_path.why_valid: The reported projectile result is a consequence of one component model and one event, so its components must refer to the same instant and satisfy a_x=0, a_y=-g.
teaching_path.output: checked projectile consequence at one physical event

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A projectile needs a horizontal force to keep moving horizontally.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If a_x=0 after release, can v_x still be nonzero?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Zero horizontal acceleration means horizontal velocity stays constant, not that it becomes zero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A horizontal launch has no vertical velocity throughout the flight.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: One second after a horizontal launch, is v_y still zero under gravity?
misconceptions.repair: No. u_y=0 only at release; a_y=-g makes v_y=-gt afterward.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: At the highest point the whole velocity and the acceleration are both zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At the apex of an oblique projectile, which of v_x, v_y and a_y is zero?
misconceptions.repair: Only v_y is zero at that instant. v_x remains u_x and a_y remains -g.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Same-height flight formulas may be used whenever the question is about a projectile range or flight time.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A ball launched from a roof lands on the ground below. May the same-height time-of-flight shortcut be used without checking the vertical displacement?
misconceptions.repair: No. Same-height shortcuts require Delta y=0 between launch and landing. For unequal heights, solve the vertical position condition.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: At two points of the same height on an ideal trajectory, the velocity vectors are identical.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: On ascent and descent at the same height, how do the horizontal and vertical velocity components compare?
misconceptions.repair: v_x is the same, while v_y has equal magnitude and opposite sign; the speed matches but the velocity vector does not.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Horizontal speed determines how long a horizontally launched object takes to fall.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If the horizontal launch speed doubles from the same height, does the ideal fall time change?
misconceptions.repair: No. The vertical position equation determines the fall time; horizontal speed changes the range, not the fall time.

exit_task.prompt: A stone is launched horizontally from a cliff with speed u. With +y upward and air resistance neglected, write its component acceleration, velocity and displacement relations after release and explain why one common t is used.

answer.summary: a_x=0, a_y=-g; v_x=u, v_y=-gt; Delta x=ut, Delta y=-0.5gt², all at the same elapsed time t.
reasoning: After release only gravity acts in the ideal model.
Gravity has no horizontal component in the chosen frame.
Both component coordinates describe the same stone at the same instant.
answer.check: Horizontal velocity remains constant while downward speed magnitude grows with time.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit task is symbolic and model-based; no cliff height or numerical g is required.

microtopics.research_contribution: Selected ExamSIDE horizontal/oblique projectile questions justify a durable projectile model capability. Range, height and time-of-flight remain consequences/variations, not separate capabilities.

predict.prompt: Immediately after a horizontal launch, which acceleration component is zero in the ideal model?
predict.defensible_answer: a_x is zero; a_y is -g if +y is upward.

attempt.produces: A model declaration and component-equation setup for a horizontal or oblique projectile.

rubric.criterion: The learner selects gravity-only free flight, uses a_x=0/a_y=-g and one common time before calculating any named projectile quantity.
rubric.evidence_of: Projectile model selection rather than formula recall.

accepted: State assumptions, set component accelerations, then solve x/y with one t.
rejected: Start from a memorized range/height formula without establishing the free-flight component model.

route.ask: What forces remain after release in the idealized problem?
route.why_this_ask: Elicits the gravity-only model.

route.ask: What are the horizontal and vertical component equations, and what clock do they share?
route.why_this_ask: Rebuilds the projectile specialization from 2D constant acceleration.

route.ask: What exact component condition identifies the event the question asks about?
route.why_this_ask: Separates model selection from event selection.

route.ask: If the event is the apex, what becomes zero and what definitely does not?
route.why_this_ask: Protects against the common full-velocity/full-acceleration zero shortcut.

route.ask: Does launch height equal landing height? If not, which shortcut becomes invalid?
route.why_this_ask: Makes the same-height boundary explicit.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: Teaching states the projectile specialization; reconstruction derives it from the post-release interaction model and coordinate choice.

boundary_test.prompt: A launched object continues under significant horizontal thrust after release. May the standard a_x=0 projectile specialization be used?
boundary_test.answer: No. The object is not in gravity-only free flight; its horizontal acceleration is not zero under that model.
boundary_test.confirms: Projectile equations are conditional consequences of a declared force/model state.

relations.expression: v_x = u_x + a_x t; v_y = u_y + a_y t
relations.meaning: Each perpendicular velocity component follows the 1D constant-acceleration relation over one common interval.
conditions: a_x and a_y are constant over the interval.
Both component equations use the same elapsed time and frame.

derivation.action: Apply the existing constant-acceleration velocity relation v=u+at along the x axis only.
derivation.why_valid: The x component is one one-dimensional constant-acceleration motion when a_x is constant.

derivation.action: Apply the same relation independently along the y axis over the same elapsed time.
derivation.why_valid: The y component has its own constant acceleration a_y but describes the same event interval.

derivation.action: Read the two equations together as one velocity component pair at time t.
derivation.why_valid: The component pair represents one plane velocity only when frame and time agree.
derivation.output: v(t) has components (u_x+a_x t, u_y+a_y t)

limits: If either acceleration component varies during the interval, that component's constant-acceleration velocity equation is not exact over the whole interval.
These component equations do not by themselves select the coordinate frame or determine whether acceleration is constant.
checks: Units match velocity on both equations.
If a_x=0 then v_x stays constant; likewise for y.

relations.expression: Delta x = u_x t + 0.5 a_x t^2; Delta y = u_y t + 0.5 a_y t^2
relations.meaning: Each perpendicular displacement component follows the 1D constant-acceleration displacement relation over one common interval.
conditions: a_x and a_y are constant over the interval.
Both component equations use the same elapsed time and frame.

derivation.action: Apply the existing constant-acceleration displacement relation Delta s=u t+0.5 a t^2 to the x component.
derivation.why_valid: The x displacement is a one-dimensional component motion with initial velocity u_x and constant acceleration a_x.
derivation.output: Delta x = u_x t + 0.5 a_x t^2

derivation.action: Apply the same relation to the y component using the same elapsed time.
derivation.why_valid: The y component evolves independently but belongs to the same physical interval.
derivation.output: Delta y = u_y t + 0.5 a_y t^2

derivation.action: Recombine the two signed displacements as one plane displacement.
derivation.why_valid: A Cartesian displacement is determined by its signed perpendicular components.
derivation.output: Delta r has components (u_x t+0.5 a_x t^2, u_y t+0.5 a_y t^2)

limits: The displacement component equations require constant a_x and a_y over the interval on which each one is used.
They describe displacement from the chosen initial instant, not total path length.
checks: Every term has length units.
Setting one acceleration component to zero reduces that axis to uniform motion.

relations.expression: a_x = 0; a_y = -g; v_x = u_x; v_y = u_y - g t; Delta x = u_x t; Delta y = u_y t - 0.5 g t^2
relations.meaning: With +y upward, air resistance neglected and near-Earth constant g, projectile motion is 2D constant acceleration specialized to zero horizontal and downward vertical acceleration.
conditions: Near-Earth region with approximately constant g.
Air resistance neglected.
+y is declared upward for the displayed signs.
The object is in free flight after release.

derivation.action: For free flight near Earth with air resistance neglected and +y upward, set a_x=0 and a_y=-g.
derivation.why_valid: Gravity is the only retained acceleration in the ideal projectile model and points vertically downward.

derivation.action: Substitute a_x=0 and a_y=-g into the 2D velocity component relations.
derivation.why_valid: The projectile model is a specialization of the same component constant-acceleration equations.
derivation.output: v_x = u_x; v_y = u_y - g t

derivation.action: Substitute the same acceleration components into the 2D displacement relations.
derivation.why_valid: Horizontal and vertical displacements follow the same specialized component model over the shared time.
derivation.output: Delta x = u_x t; Delta y = u_y t - 0.5 g t^2

derivation.action: Check that horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes linearly with time.
derivation.why_valid: Those trends follow directly from a_x=0 and a_y=-g.
derivation.output: constant v_x and linearly decreasing v_y under the declared +y-up convention

limits: The displayed projectile specialization is not exact when drag, propulsion, contact forces, appreciably varying g or a rotating-frame effect is material.
Changing the vertical sign convention changes the displayed signs; the physical downward acceleration does not change.
checks: v_x is constant.
At the highest point of an oblique trajectory, v_y=0 but a_y remains -g.
Both component equations use the same t.
